IMPORTANT NOTICE: This deed must be recorded in the county where the property is located on or before 60 days after the date it is notarized, or it will not be effective.

clauses.title: Notice Details
clauses.body: NOTICE TO PAY RENT OR QUIT. To: {{tenantName}}. Property: {{propertyAddress}}. Date of this notice: {{noticeDate}}. {{landlordName}}, as landlord, states that rent in the amount of ${{rentOwed}} is now due and unpaid for the property described above. Within three (3) days after service of this notice, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and other judicial holidays, {{tenantName}} must pay the full amount stated above or deliver possession of the property. Failure to do either within that period may result in legal proceedings to recover possession of the property.

clauses.title: The Three-Day Notice: How the Period Is Counted
clauses.body: Under California statute, a tenant is guilty of unlawful detainer when the tenant continues in possession, without the landlord's permission, after default in payment of rent due under the lease, and the landlord has served a written three-day notice requiring payment of the rent or possession of the property, stating the amount due. The three days are counted excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and other judicial holidays — so a notice served on a Friday does not expire until the following Wednesday at the earliest (assuming no intervening holiday), not the following Monday. The notice may be served at any time within one year after the rent becomes due.
clauses.gap: This is California's statutory rule (Code of Civil Procedure section 1161, paragraph 2), not a rule that applies in every state — eviction notice periods, and how they are counted, vary by state, and some states count all calendar days rather than excluding weekends and holidays. This document addresses California's statewide statute only; it does not cover any city or county's local rent-control or eviction ordinance, and many California cities (San Francisco, Los Angeles, Oakland, and others) layer their own, often stricter, notice and just-cause requirements on top of this statewide floor. The "excluding Saturdays and Sundays and other judicial holidays" counting method was added to this paragraph by legislation effective September 1, 2019, replacing a rule that had counted all calendar days; that counting method remains in the statute's text as most recently amended, effective February 1, 2025, confirming it is still the operative rule as of the date this research was checked. The one-year service window and the three-day countdown are two distinct time limits within the same statutory paragraph, not independent sources, and are disclosed together here for that reason.

citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, the three-day notice requirement and weekend/holiday exclusion
citations.quote: When the tenant continues in possession, in person or by subtenant, without the permission of the landlord, or the successor in estate of the landlord, if applicable, after default in the payment of rent, pursuant to the lease or agreement under which the property is held, and three days' notice, excluding Saturdays and Sundays and other judicial holidays, in writing, requiring its payment, stating the amount that is due... or possession of the property, shall have been served upon the tenant and if there is a subtenant in actual occupation of the premises, also upon the subtenant.

citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, the one-year window for serving the notice
citations.quote: The notice may be served at any time within one year after the rent becomes due.

clauses.title: Required Contents of the Notice
clauses.body: California's unlawful-detainer statute specifies what a three-day notice for nonpayment of rent must state: the amount of rent that is due, and the name, telephone number, and address of the person to whom the rent payment should be made. If payment may be made in person, the notice must also state the usual days and hours that person will be available to receive it. The statute additionally allows the notice to identify a financial-institution account (if the institution is within five miles of the rental property) or an electronic-funds-transfer procedure, if one is already established, as an alternative way to pay. California courts have held that a three-day notice under this statute is valid only if it strictly complies with these statutory requirements, and that a notice demanding more rent than is actually owed is defective.
clauses.gap: This is California's statutory content checklist (Code of Civil Procedure section 1161, paragraph 2) and California case law construing it; both apply only to a tenancy governed by California law, and the specific items a notice must contain to be valid vary by state. This document covers the statewide requirement only — it does not address any additional content a specific city or county ordinance might require. The "strict compliance" rule quoted below comes from a published California Court of Appeal decision (Kwok v. Bergren, 1982), an independent source from the statute itself, not merely a different subsection of section 1161.

citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, the statutory content requirements for the notice
citations.quote: three days' notice, excluding Saturdays and Sundays and other judicial holidays, in writing, requiring its payment, stating the amount that is due, the name, telephone number, and address of the person to whom the rent payment shall be made, and, if payment may be made personally, the usual days and hours that person will be available to receive the payment (provided that, if the address does not allow for personal delivery, then it shall be conclusively presumed that upon the mailing of any rent or notice to the owner by the tenant to the name and address provided, the notice or rent is deemed received by the owner on the date posted, if the tenant can show proof of mailing to the name and address provided by the owner), or the number of an account in a financial institution into which the rental payment may be made, and the name and street address of the institution (provided that the institution is located within five miles of the rental property), or if an electronic funds transfer procedure has been previously established, that payment may be made pursuant to that procedure, or possession of the property, shall have been served upon the tenant and if there is a subtenant in actual occupation of the premises, also upon the subtenant.

An unlawful detainer action is not based upon contract...; it is a statutory proceeding and is governed solely by the provisions of the statute creating it... a lessor's action to recover possession of real property is not one for unlawful detainer where he does not comply with the statutory notice requirements.

clauses.title: How the Notice May Be Served
clauses.body: California statute prescribes three permitted methods for serving this notice on a residential tenant, to be used in this order of preference: (1) personal delivery to the tenant; (2) if the tenant cannot be found at home or at their usual place of business, leaving a copy with a person of suitable age and discretion at either place and also mailing a copy to the tenant's residence; or (3) if neither the tenant's residence nor place of business can be determined, or no person of suitable age or discretion can be found there, posting a copy in a conspicuous place on the property and mailing a copy to the property address — commonly called "nail and mail" — while also handing a copy to anyone else found residing there. If a subtenant is in actual occupation of the property, service must also be made on the subtenant.
clauses.gap: This is California's statutory list of proper service methods (Code of Civil Procedure section 1162(a)) for the notice described elsewhere in this document; other states authorize different service methods, and some require methods this statute does not (such as certified mail alone). This document addresses the statewide method only — some California cities impose additional local service or documentation requirements on top of it. The statute also sets out a separate set of service methods for a commercial tenant, in a different subdivision of this same section, which this document does not address because it concerns residential tenancies. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 1162(a)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, the permitted methods of serving the notice on a residential tenant
citations.quote: Except as provided in subdivision (b), the notices required by Sections 1161 and 1161a may be served by any of the following methods: (1) By delivering a copy to the tenant personally. (2) If he or she is absent from his or her place of residence, and from his or her usual place of business, by leaving a copy with some person of suitable age and discretion at either place, and sending a copy through the mail addressed to the tenant at his or her place of residence. (3) If such place of residence and business cannot be ascertained, or a person of suitable age or discretion there can not be found, then by affixing a copy in a conspicuous place on the property, and also delivering a copy to a person there residing, if such person can be found; and also sending a copy through the mail addressed to the tenant at the place where the property is situated. Service upon a subtenant may be made in the same manner.

clauses.title: The Tenant's Right to Pay and Avoid Eviction
clauses.body: The three-day notice is written, by statute, as a choice: it requires "its payment... or possession of the property." A tenant who pays the full amount the notice states is due, within the three-day period, has complied with the notice, and the nonpayment ground for unlawful detainer described in the statute does not arise. In the neighboring paragraph of the same statute, covering a tenant's failure to perform other lease conditions or covenants, the Legislature has spelled this principle out expressly: within the three-day period, the tenant "may perform the conditions or covenants of the lease or pay the stipulated rent, as the case may be, and thereby save the lease from forfeiture."
clauses.gap: This is California statute (Code of Civil Procedure section 1161); the cure period, and whether curing avoids eviction at all, both vary by state. This document addresses California's statewide rule only, not any city or county's local ordinance. Both citations below come from the same statutory section — paragraph (2), covering rent default, and paragraph (3), covering other lease-covenant defaults — rather than independent sources; no additional independent source was found. Notably, the express "save the lease from forfeiture" sentence, quoted above, appears in paragraph (3)'s text governing other covenant breaches, not paragraph (2)'s rent-default text; paragraph (3)'s own wording nonetheless refers to a tenant choosing to "pay the stipulated rent... as the case may be" as one of the two ways to avoid forfeiture, so the same underlying principle — timely payment defeats the unlawful detainer claim — is expressed in both places, just not in identical sentences. This document states that structural fact rather than treating the two paragraphs as saying exactly the same thing.

citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, the notice's payment-or-possession structure
citations.quote: three days' notice, excluding Saturdays and Sundays and other judicial holidays, in writing, requiring its payment, stating the amount that is due... or possession of the property, shall have been served upon the tenant

citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, the express statutory cure-and-save-from-forfeiture language
citations.quote: Within three days, excluding Saturdays and Sundays and other judicial holidays, after the service of the notice, the tenant, or any subtenant in actual occupation of the premises, or any mortgagee of the term, or other person interested in its continuance, may perform the conditions or covenants of the lease or pay the stipulated rent, as the case may be, and thereby save the lease from forfeiture; provided, if the conditions and covenants of the lease, violated by the lessee, cannot afterward be performed, then no notice, as last prescribed herein, need be given to the lessee or the subtenant, demanding the performance of the violated conditions or covenants of the lease.

clauses.title: Nonpayment of Rent Under California's Statewide Just-Cause Law
clauses.body: Since 2020, California's Tenant Protection Act has required a landlord to have "just cause," stated in the written termination notice, to end certain tenancies once a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a unit for 12 months (or, in some multi-tenant situations, 24 months). Default in the payment of rent is specifically listed in the statute as one form of "at-fault just cause." Unlike some other at-fault violations under this law, a landlord is not required to give a separate advance notice-and-cure step before serving a nonpayment three-day notice — the three-day pay-or-quit notice described elsewhere in this document is itself the notice the statute contemplates for a rent default. The Tenant Protection Act's just-cause requirement does not apply to every California tenancy: the statute lists a number of specific exemptions, including (among others) certain single-family owner-occupied residences, certain small two-unit owner-occupied properties, housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the preceding 15 years, and housing meeting specified individually-alienable-title and non-corporate-ownership conditions paired with a required written exemption notice to the tenant. This statewide just-cause requirement is currently scheduled to expire, and be repealed, on January 1, 2030.
clauses.gap: This is a California statewide statute (Civil Code section 1946.2), not a rule that exists in every state, and the exemption list above is a summary, not a complete restatement — the statute's exemption paragraph runs to nine numbered categories with detailed sub-conditions attached to several of them (for example, the single-family and small-property exemptions carry specific occupancy and unit-count conditions, and the individually-alienable-title exemption requires a specific written notice using statutory language), and this document does not attempt to reproduce every condition. A related statute, Civil Code section 1947.12, caps how much rent can be increased over a 12-month period for many of the same tenancies; it governs rent increases, not the eviction-notice process, so it is not reproduced here, but it exists alongside the just-cause rule as part of the same legislative package. This document addresses statewide California law only; a number of California cities and counties have their own local rent-control and just-cause ordinances that impose additional or different requirements on top of the statewide law, and this document does not cover any of them. All citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (Civil Code section 1946.2) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was used for this clause.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, the statewide just-cause requirement
citations.quote: Notwithstanding any other law, after a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a residential real property for 12 months, the owner of the residential real property shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause, which shall be stated in the written notice to terminate tenancy.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, nonpayment of rent as at-fault just cause
citations.quote: For purposes of this section, 'just cause' means either of the following: (1) At-fault just cause, which means any of the following: (A) Default in the payment of rent.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, the separate cure-notice step that applies to other curable lease violations but not to a rent default
citations.quote: Before an owner of residential real property issues a notice to terminate a tenancy for just cause that is a curable lease violation, the owner shall first give notice of the violation to the tenant with an opportunity to cure the violation pursuant to paragraph (3) of Section 1161 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, the just-cause law's stated exemptions
citations.quote: This section shall not apply to the following types of residential real properties or residential circumstances: (1) Transient and tourist hotel occupancy as defined in subdivision (b) of Section 1940. (2) Housing accommodations in a nonprofit hospital, religious facility, extended care facility, licensed residential care facility for the elderly... or an adult residential facility... (3) Dormitories owned and operated by an institution of higher education or a kindergarten and grades 1 to 12, inclusive, school. (4) Housing accommodations in which the tenant shares bathroom or kitchen facilities with the owner who maintains their principal residence at the residential real property. (5) Single-family owner-occupied residences, including both of the following: (A) A residence in which the owner-occupant rents or leases no more than two units or bedrooms... (B) A mobilehome. (6) A property containing two separate dwelling units within a single structure in which the owner occupied one of the units as the owner's principal place of residence at the beginning of the tenancy, so long as the owner continues in occupancy... (7) Housing that has been issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years, unless the housing is a mobilehome. (8) Residential real property, including a mobilehome, that is alienable separate from the title to any other dwelling unit, provided that both of the following apply: (A) The owner is not any of the following: (i) A real estate investment trust... (ii) A corporation. (iii) A limited liability company in which at least one member is a corporation. (iv) Management of a mobilehome park... (B) The tenants have been provided written notice that the residential property is exempt from this section... (9) Housing restricted by deed, regulatory restriction contained in an agreement with a government agency, or other recorded document as affordable housing for persons and families of very low, low, or moderate income...

citations.cite: California Civil Code, the just-cause law's own sunset date
citations.quote: This section shall remain in effect only until January 1, 2030, and as of that date is repealed.

clauses.title: COVID-19-Era Notice Modifications: Current Status
clauses.body: California enacted temporary COVID-19-era eviction protections beginning in 2020, including a period during which nonpayment notices for COVID-19 rental debt required a longer notice period and specific tenant-facing declarations rather than the standard three-day notice. Those temporary statutes carried their own expiration dates. As of the date this document's sourcing was checked, no COVID-19-era modification to the notice period or notice contents remains in the currently codified text governing this notice: the operative statute is the version of Code of Civil Procedure section 1161 most recently amended effective February 1, 2025, and its text imposes the standard three-day (weekend/holiday-excluded) notice period described elsewhere in this document, with no COVID-19-related exception or extended period.
clauses.gap: This is a currency check against California's currently codified statute, not a claim that no COVID-19-related eviction rule was ever adopted anywhere — other states and some California cities may have adopted their own, separate protections on different timelines, and this document does not track those. The finding here rests on direct review of the current text of the statute that would carry any such modification if one still applied (Code of Civil Procedure section 1161), which contains no COVID-19-related provision; direct lookups of the specific code sections that had carried California's now-expired COVID-19 tenant relief provisions (Code of Civil Procedure section 1179.01 and a related Civil Code section in the 1179 series, added in 2020) returned no codified text at those citations, consistent with those provisions having sunset and been removed from the code rather than merely amended. This is reported as a negative finding based on direct source review, not a claim independently verified against a repealing bill's legislative history. This is a single statutory citation (§ 1161); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, current operative text and amendment history showing no COVID-19-era modification remains
citations.quote: (Amended (as added by Stats. 2020, Ch. 37, Sec. 16) by Stats. 2024, Ch. 287, Sec. 6. (SB 611) Effective January 1, 2025. Operative February 1, 2025, by its own provisions.)

clauses.title: Payment Instructions
clauses.body: Rent payment under this notice should be made to: {{paymentPayeeName}}, telephone {{paymentPhone}}, at {{paymentAddress}}. If payment may be made in person, the usual days and hours available to receive payment are: {{paymentHours}}. Payment may also be made by any other method the parties have previously and separately agreed to in writing, including an established electronic funds transfer procedure or a designated financial institution account.

clauses.title: Landlord Signature and Declaration of Service
clauses.body:
Signed: {{landlordName}}, Landlord. Date: _______________.

Declaration of Service. This notice was served on {{tenantName}} on _______________ (date), by the following method (check one): ☐ personal delivery to the tenant; ☐ leaving a copy with a person of suitable age and discretion at the tenant's residence or usual place of business, together with mailing a copy to the tenant's residence; ☐ posting a copy in a conspicuous place on the property and mailing a copy to the property address, after the tenant's residence and place of business could not be ascertained or no person of suitable age or discretion could be found there.

Served by: _______________ (name) Date: _______________

clauses.title: Tax Treatment of Founder Stock Subject to Vesting
clauses.body: When a founder receives stock or another form of equity in {{companyName}} that is subject to a vesting schedule, federal tax law generally does not tax that equity's value at the time of grant. Instead, the value is included in the founder's taxable income later — in the year the equity becomes vested or freely transferable, based on its fair market value at that later time, not its value at grant. This is the default rule; it applies unless the founder makes a timely election under a separate provision of the same statute, described elsewhere in this document.
clauses.gap: This is federal tax law (26 U.S.C. § 83(a)) and applies the same way regardless of which state governs a specific company's formation or this agreement — it is a separate body of law from the state-law rules on entity formation and fiduciary duty addressed elsewhere in this document. This clause states the general default rule only; it does not determine the fair market value of any specific grant of equity, which is a factual question this clause does not resolve. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 83(a)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.cite: Internal Revenue Code, general rule for property transferred in connection with performance of services
citations.quote: If, in connection with the performance of services, property is transferred to any person other than the person for whom such services are performed, the excess of— (1) the fair market value of such property (determined without regard to any restriction other than a restriction which by its terms will never lapse) at the first time the rights of the person having the beneficial interest in such property are transferable or are not subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture, whichever occurs earlier, over (2) the amount (if any) paid for such property, shall be included in the gross income of the person who performed such services in the first taxable year in which the rights of the person having the beneficial interest in such property are transferable or are not subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture, whichever is applicable. The preceding sentence shall not apply if such person sells or otherwise disposes of such property in an arm's length transaction before his rights in such property become transferable or not subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture.

clauses.title: What Makes Equity "Subject to Vesting" for Tax Purposes
clauses.body: The same federal statute that governs when vesting equity is taxed also defines the condition that makes equity count as subject to vesting in the first place: a "substantial risk of forfeiture." Equity meets that test when the founder's right to keep it fully is conditioned on that founder performing future services for {{companyName}} — the same structure a typical multi-year, service-based vesting schedule uses. Whether a specific grant of equity meets this statutory test is a question of fact about how that particular grant is structured, not a label this document assigns.
clauses.gap: This is one subsection of the same federal statute cited in the clause above (26 U.S.C. § 83) — not an independent source, and disclosed as such. It is federal law and applies regardless of which state governs a specific company's formation. This clause defines the statutory test only; it does not determine whether any particular equity grant satisfies it.

citations.cite: Internal Revenue Code, definition of "substantial risk of forfeiture"
citations.quote: The rights of a person in property are subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture if such person's rights to full enjoyment of such property are conditioned upon the future performance of substantial services by any individual.

clauses.title: The Section 83(b) Election and Its 30-Day Deadline
clauses.body: Federal tax law allows a person who receives equity subject to vesting to elect to be taxed on that equity's value at the time of grant instead of waiting until it vests. This is commonly called an "83(b) election," after the statutory subsection that creates it. If made, the general vesting-based timing rule described above does not apply to that equity, and if the equity is later forfeited before it vests, no tax deduction is allowed for the amount that was already included in income because of the election. An 83(b) election, if made, must be filed not later than 30 days after the date the equity is transferred, and once made, it cannot be revoked except with the consent of the IRS.
clauses.gap: This is federal tax law (26 U.S.C. § 83(b)) and applies the same way regardless of which state governs a specific company's formation or this agreement. The regulation cited alongside the statute below independently restates the same 30-day deadline — the two sources are not fully independent of each other on that specific point, since the regulation implements the statute, and that overlap is disclosed here rather than presented as two unrelated confirmations. The regulation's text also carries a parenthetical referencing "January 29, 1970," a leftover from when the regulation was first adopted; it has no effect on a transfer occurring now, since any current transfer date is later than that fixed 1970 date, leaving the 30-day rule as the operative deadline. Separately, the regulation (not quoted in full here) also specifies required content for the election statement and requires copies to be delivered to the company — procedural detail this clause does not restate. This document does not itself file an election with the IRS or track whether one has been filed; it states the deadline as a matter of law only.

citations.cite: Internal Revenue Code, election to include property's value in gross income in the year of transfer
citations.quote: Any person who performs services in connection with which property is transferred to any person may elect to include in his gross income for the taxable year in which such property is transferred, the excess of— (A) the fair market value of such property at the time of transfer (determined without regard to any restriction other than a restriction which by its terms will never lapse), over (B) the amount (if any) paid for such property. If such election is made, subsection (a) shall not apply with respect to the transfer of such property, and if such property is subsequently forfeited, no deduction shall be allowed in respect of such forfeiture. (2) Election An election under paragraph (1) with respect to any transfer of property shall be made in such manner as the Secretary prescribes and shall be made not later than 30 days after the date of such transfer. Such election may not be revoked except with the consent of the Secretary.

citations.cite: Treasury Regulations, time for making a section 83(b) election
citations.quote: Time for making election. Except as provided in the following sentence, the election referred to in paragraph (a) of this section shall be filed not later than 30 days after the date the property was transferred (or, if later, January 29, 1970) and may be filed prior to the date of transfer. Any statement filed before February 15, 1970, which was amended not later than February 16, 1970, in order to make it conform to the requirements of paragraph (e) of this section, shall be deemed a proper election under section 83(b).

clauses.title: Work-for-Hire Baseline for Founder-Created IP
clauses.body: Work a founder creates for {{companyName}} within the scope of an actual employment relationship with {{companyName}} is generally owned by {{companyName}} automatically, under the "work made for hire" doctrine — the same default that applies to any employee's work product. That default depends on the founder actually being an employee under the law's test, not on titles: courts weigh factors including who controls the manner and means of the work, who supplies tools and workspace, how the work is paid for, and whether the person receives employee benefits and employee tax treatment. Work created outside an actual employment relationship — including by a founder acting as a contractor, advisor, or in some other non-employee capacity — is not automatically owned by {{companyName}} under this doctrine.
clauses.gap: This clause restates, for the founder context, the same federal copyright doctrine and the same primary-source quotes already verified in this project's Invention Assignment & Confidentiality Agreement document (reused verbatim, not re-fetched, per this project's source-reuse practice). It does not by itself resolve the separate question — addressed in the next clause — of work a founder created before a specific company existed as a legal entity.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, ownership of work made for hire
citations.quote: In the case of a work made for hire, the employer or other person for whom the work was prepared is considered the author for purposes of this title, and, unless the parties have expressly agreed otherwise in a written instrument signed by them, owns all of the rights comprised in the copyright.

citations.case: Community for Creative Non-Violence v. Reid
citations.quote: In determining whether a hired party is an employee under the general common law of agency, we consider the hiring party's right to control the manner and means by which the product is accomplished.

Some factors, therefore, will often have little or no significance in determining whether a party is an independent contractor or an employee. In contrast, there are some factors that will be significant in virtually every situation. These include: (1) the hiring party's right to control the manner and means of creation; (2) the skill required; (3) the provision of employee benefits; (4) the tax treatment of the hired party; and (5) whether the hiring party has the right to assign additional projects to the hired party. These factors will almost always be relevant and should be given more weight in the analysis, because they will usually be highly probative of the true nature of the employment relationship.

clauses.title: Pre-Incorporation and Pre-Signing Work Is a Different Question
clauses.body: Work a founder created before {{companyName}} existed as a legal entity, or before this agreement was signed, is not automatically transferred to {{companyName}} by the work-for-hire doctrine described above. That doctrine turns on an actual employer-employee relationship existing at the time the work was created, and an entity that had not yet been formed cannot have been anyone's employer during that period. Ownership of work created before {{companyName}}'s formation generally remains with the individual founder who created it unless and until that founder expressly assigns it — assignment does not happen automatically just because the founder later joins, works for, or holds equity in {{companyName}}.
clauses.gap: This point follows from the definition of "employer" already built into the work-for-hire doctrine cited in the clause above (17 U.S.C. § 101/201(b) and the Reid agency test) — it is not an independently codified California or federal rule specifically addressing pre-incorporation founder IP, and no such distinct statute or clean holding was found in this research. One federal bankruptcy court decision illustrates the practical stakes: in a dispute where a founder had developed the underlying invention before the company was incorporated and never signed an assignment, the company had to establish ownership through a fact-intensive fiduciary-duty and conduct-based theory rather than automatic operation of law. That case did not apply California law — it involved a Delaware corporation and was decided by a Massachusetts federal bankruptcy court — so it is offered here only as an illustration of the risk that assignment gaps create, not as California authority or as a general rule that pre-incorporation IP is always the founder's personal property. This is a single case; no additional independent source was found for this specific illustration.

citations.case: Access Cardiosystems, Inc. v. Fincke (In re Access Cardiosystems, Inc.)
citations.cite: 340 B.R. 127 (Bankr. D. Mass. 2006)
citations.quote: In spite of the fact that Fincke, as the named inventor on the '645 Application, was the de facto owner of the invention disclosed in the '645 Application and any patent to be issued, no licensing agreement was ever entered into between Fincke and Access regarding Access's use of the intellectual property.

clauses.title: Which Fiduciary-Duty Statute Applies Depends on How Founders Have Organized
clauses.body: Founders do not owe each other the same fiduciary duties automatically, regardless of what business structure they use — which statute applies depends on the entity form chosen. If founders are operating as a general partnership (including, potentially, by default before any formal entity is created), each partner owes a statutory duty of loyalty and a duty of care to the partnership and the other partners. If founders instead form a corporation, that partnership statute does not apply to them as founders — a corporation's directors instead owe duties defined by a separate statute governing corporate directors, requiring good faith, a reasonable belief that their actions serve the corporation's and shareholders' best interests, and the care an ordinarily prudent person would use in a like position. If founders form an LLC, a third, separate statute applies: in a member-managed LLC, members owe a duty of loyalty and duty of care similar in structure to the partnership duties; in a manager-managed LLC, those duties shift to the manager or managers, and a member who is not also a manager owes no fiduciary duty to the company or the other members solely because of being a member.
clauses.gap: These are three genuinely separate California statutes, each addressing a different entity form — that separation is disclosed here rather than treated as one combined rule. Each is one state's statute, offered as evidence of California's default structure for the relevant entity type — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific company, and not a determination of which entity form a specific company has actually chosen. The partnership and LLC citations below were previously verified for this project's Partnership Agreement and LLC Operating Agreement documents and are reused verbatim here rather than re-fetched; the corporate-director citation was independently fetched and verified for this document. This clause does not resolve which entity type applies to a specific group of founders, and does not address the fact-specific question of whether founders who have not yet formed any entity might be treated as a de facto general partnership under California law before formal organization — that determination depends on facts this clause does not evaluate.

citations.cite: California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, the two fiduciary duties a partner owes
citations.quote: (a) The fiduciary duties a partner owes to the partnership and the other partners are the duty of loyalty and the duty of care set forth in subdivisions (b) and (c).

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, a director's standard of conduct
citations.quote: A director shall perform the duties of a director, including duties as a member of any committee of the board upon which the director may serve, in good faith, in a manner such director believes to be in the best interests of the corporation and its shareholders and with such care, including reasonable inquiry, as an ordinarily prudent person in a like position would use under similar circumstances.

citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, duties shift to the manager in a manager-managed LLC
citations.quote: In a manager-managed limited liability company, all of the following rules apply: (1) Subdivisions (a), (b), (c), and (e) apply to the manager or managers and not the members. (2) Subdivision (d) applies to the members and managers. (3) Except as otherwise provided, a member does not have any fiduciary duty to the limited liability company or to any other member solely by reason of being a member.

clauses.title: A Founder's Status as an Employee Is Still At-Will by Default
clauses.body: When a founder also works for {{companyName}} as an employee — common in early-stage companies — California's default employment rule still applies to that role: employment with no specified term may be ended by either party, on notice to the other, at any time and without cause. Founder status, equity ownership, or a title such as "co-founder" does not by itself change this default. The default can be modified only by an express or implied agreement establishing enforceable expectations about the term of employment or the grounds or manner of termination; absent such an agreement, the at-will default controls.
clauses.gap: This is one state's default employment rule (Cal. Labor Code § 2922) and applies only to a founder's separate status as an employee of a specific company, not to that founder's equity ownership or governance rights, which are addressed elsewhere in this document. The case cited alongside the statute discusses and applies the same statutory section, so its first quoted passage is not fully independent of the statute on that narrow point — that overlap is disclosed here. The case's second quoted passage adds genuinely separate content: it is itself quoting a different, earlier California Court of Appeal decision (Pugh v. See's Candies, Inc., 116 Cal.App.3d 311) to describe how the at-will presumption can be rebutted by an implied agreement, based on factors such as personnel policies, an employee's length of service, and employer assurances of continued employment — this clause does not evaluate whether such factors are present in any specific case.

citations.cite: California Labor Code, at-will employment default
citations.quote: An employment, having no specified term, may be terminated at the will of either party on notice to the other. Employment for a specified term means an employment for a period greater than one month.

Pursuant to Labor Code section 2922, if the parties reach no express or implied agreement to the contrary, the relationship is terminable at any time without cause. But when the parties have enforceable expectations concerning either the term of employment or the grounds or manner of termination, Labor Code section 2922 does not diminish the force of such contractual or legal obligations. The presumption that an employment relationship of indefinite duration is intended to be terminable at will is therefore "subject, like any presumption, to contrary evidence. This may take the form of an agreement, express or implied, that . . . the employment relationship will continue indefinitely, pending the occurrence of some event such as the employer's dissatisfaction with the employee's services or the existence of some 'cause' for termination."

clauses.title: Deposit Details
clauses.body: SECURITY DEPOSIT ITEMIZATION / MOVE-OUT STATEMENT. Landlord: {{landlordName}}. Tenant: {{tenantName}}. Property: {{propertyAddress}}. Security deposit received: ${{depositAmount}}, received on or about {{moveInDate}}. Tenant vacated the property on {{moveOutDate}}. This statement is dated {{statementDate}} and sets out the disposition of the security deposit described above.

clauses.title: The Statutory Cap on the Deposit Amount
clauses.body: Under California statute, a landlord generally may not demand or receive a security deposit, however denominated, in excess of one month's rent, in addition to the first month's rent paid on or before initial occupancy. A narrower exception permits a higher cap of two months' rent, but only for a landlord who is a natural person (or an LLC whose members are all natural persons) and who owns no more than two residential rental properties totaling no more than four dwelling units offered for rent combined — and even that higher cap does not apply if the prospective tenant is a service member, in which case the one-month cap still controls. This general one-month cap took effect for security collected or demanded on or after July 1, 2024; it does not apply to security collected or demanded before that date. Separately, and not subject to the cap described above, a landlord may require an advance rent payment of not less than six months' rent if the lease term is six months or longer.
clauses.gap: This is California's current statutory cap, not a nationwide figure — security deposit caps vary enormously by state, from no state-level cap at all to caps expressed in different terms, and this document tracks California's statewide statute only, not the pre-July 2024 two- or three-month caps that used to apply generally and that a reader may have seen referenced in older material. This document addresses California's statewide statute only; it does not cover any city or county's local rent-control or security-deposit ordinance that might impose its own, different rule. All citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (Civil Code § 1950.5) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, general one-month security deposit cap
citations.quote: a landlord shall not demand or receive security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of an amount equal to one month's rent, in addition to any rent for the first month paid on or before initial occupancy.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, higher cap for a small individual landlord
citations.quote: a landlord shall not demand or receive security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of an amount equal to two months' rent, in addition to any rent for the first month paid on or before initial occupancy if the landlord meets both of the following requirements: (i) The landlord is a natural person or a limited liability company in which all members are natural persons. (ii) The landlord owns no more than two residential rental properties that collectively include no more than four dwelling units offered for rent.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, the small-landlord cap doesn't apply to a service-member tenant
citations.quote: Subparagraph (A) shall not apply if the prospective tenant is a service member.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, effective date of the general cap
citations.quote: This subdivision shall not apply to a security collected or demanded by the landlord before July 1, 2024.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, advance rent for a longer lease
citations.quote: This subdivision does not prohibit an advance payment of not less than six months' rent if the term of the lease is six months or longer.

clauses.title: Permitted Uses of the Deposit — and the Ordinary Wear-and-Tear Carve-Out
clauses.body: Under California statute, a security deposit may be used only for the following purposes, subject to the further limits described below: (1) compensating the landlord for a tenant's default in the payment of rent; (2) repairing damage to the premises caused by the tenant or the tenant's guest or licensee, exclusive of ordinary wear and tear; (3) cleaning the premises at the end of the tenancy, to the extent necessary to return the unit to the same level of cleanliness it was in at the start of the tenancy; and (4) remedying a future default by the tenant in an obligation to restore, replace, or return personal property or appurtenances, exclusive of ordinary wear and tear, but only if the rental agreement authorizes the deposit to be applied to that purpose. Beyond this list, a landlord may claim from the deposit only amounts that are reasonably necessary for those purposes, and may not assert a claim against the deposit for damage or a defective condition that predates the tenancy, for ordinary wear and tear or its effects (whether the wear and tear predates or occurs during the tenancy), or for the cumulative effect of ordinary wear and tear across one or more tenancies.
clauses.gap: The "ordinary wear and tear" exclusion is a real, litigated line rather than a formality — the statute repeats it separately for damage repair, for the fourth (personal-property) use, and again as an affirmative bar on any claim for wear and tear regardless of when it occurred, but the statute itself does not define what counts as "ordinary" wear and tear as opposed to tenant-caused damage; that line is drawn case by case rather than by a statutory checklist. This is one state's exhaustive statutory list — other states permit different, and sometimes broader or narrower, categories of deductions, and this document does not track any state's law but California's, and only the statewide rule, not any city or county ordinance that might narrow it further. All citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (Civil Code § 1950.5) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, the first three permitted uses of a security deposit
citations.quote: (1) The compensation of a landlord for a tenant's default in the payment of rent. (2) The repair of damages to the premises, exclusive of ordinary wear and tear, caused by the tenant or by a guest or licensee of the tenant. (3) The cleaning of the premises upon termination of the tenancy necessary to return the unit to the same level of cleanliness it was in at the inception of the tenancy.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, the fourth permitted use — future personal-property defaults
citations.quote: (4) To remedy future defaults by the tenant in any obligation under the rental agreement to restore, replace, or return personal property or appurtenances, exclusive of ordinary wear and tear, if the security deposit is authorized to be applied thereto by the rental agreement.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, the "reasonably necessary" limit on a claim
citations.quote: the landlord may claim of the security only those amounts as are reasonably necessary for the purposes specified in subdivision (b).

citations.cite: California Civil Code, the affirmative bar on a wear-and-tear or pre-existing-condition claim
citations.quote: The landlord shall not assert a claim against the tenant or the security for damages to the premises or any defective conditions that preexisted the tenancy, for ordinary wear and tear or the effects thereof, whether the wear and tear preexisted the tenancy or occurred during the tenancy, or for the cumulative effects of ordinary wear and tear occurring during any one or more tenancies.

clauses.title: The 21-Day Itemization and Refund Deadline
clauses.body: Under California statute, no later than 21 calendar days after the tenant has vacated the premises, the landlord must furnish the tenant a copy of an itemized statement indicating the basis for, and the amount of, any security received and its disposition, and must return any remaining portion of the deposit to the tenant. Along with that itemized statement, the landlord must also include copies of documents showing the charges deducted — bills, invoices, or receipts for repair or cleaning work performed by someone other than the landlord, or a description of the work and the time and hourly rate charged if the landlord or the landlord's employee performed it. If a repair cannot reasonably be completed within the 21-day period, or if supporting documents from a person or entity providing services, materials, or supplies are not yet in the landlord's possession within that period, the landlord may instead deduct a good-faith estimate of the charges and provide that estimate with the itemized statement, then complete the documentation requirements within 14 calendar days after the repair is finished or the documentation is received. A landlord need not provide supporting documents at all — for either the initial statement or the later completion — if the total deductions for repairs and cleaning combined do not exceed $125, or if the tenant has separately signed a written waiver of that documentation right.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statutory deadline and documentation threshold, not a nationwide figure — the length of the return/itemization period, and whether receipts are required at all, vary considerably by state. This document addresses California's statewide statute only, not any city or county ordinance that might impose additional or different move-out documentation requirements. The 21-day period does not start running before the landlord or tenant gives notice to terminate the tenancy (or, for a fixed-term lease, no earlier than 60 calendar days before the lease's expiration) — a timing nuance distinct from the 21-day outer deadline itself and easy to overlook. A landlord who, in bad faith, fails to comply with this itemization and documentation subdivision is not entitled to claim any amount of the security at all — a separate and more severe consequence than the general bad-faith penalty described elsewhere in this document. All citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (Civil Code § 1950.5) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, the 21-day itemization and refund deadline
citations.quote: No later than 21 calendar days after the tenant has vacated the premises, but not earlier than the time that either the landlord or the tenant provides a notice to terminate the tenancy under Section 1946 or 1946.1, Section 1161 of the Code of Civil Procedure, or not earlier than 60 calendar days prior to the expiration of a fixed-term lease, the landlord shall furnish the tenant, a copy of an itemized statement indicating the basis for, and the amount of, any security received and the disposition of the security, and shall return any remaining portion of the security to the tenant...

citations.cite: California Civil Code, the good-faith-estimate alternative when work isn't done in 21 days
citations.quote: If a repair to be done by the landlord or the landlord's employee cannot reasonably be completed within 21 calendar days after the tenant has vacated the premises, or if the documents from a person or entity providing services, materials, or supplies are not in the landlord's possession within 21 calendar days after the tenant has vacated the premises, the landlord may deduct the amount of a good faith estimate of the charges that will be incurred and provide that estimate with the itemized statement. ...Within 14 calendar days of completing the repair or receiving the documentation, the landlord shall complete the requirements in paragraphs (1) and (2) in the manner specified.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, the $125 documentation threshold
citations.quote: The landlord need not comply with paragraph (2) or (3) if either of the following applies: (A) The deductions for repairs and cleaning together do not exceed one hundred twenty-five dollars ($125).

citations.cite: California Civil Code, forfeiture for bad-faith noncompliance with this subdivision
citations.quote: The landlord shall not be entitled to claim any amount of the security if the landlord, in bad faith, fails to comply with this subdivision.

clauses.title: Itemized Deductions Schedule
Bad-Faith Retention: The Penalty for Improperly Withholding a Deposit
clauses.body: Under California statute, if a landlord (or the landlord's successor in interest) claims or retains a security deposit in bad faith, in violation of the security-deposit statute, the landlord may be liable for statutory damages of up to twice the amount of the deposit, in addition to actual damages — meaning the up-to-double penalty is added on top of whatever actual damages the tenant proves, not a cap that replaces or absorbs them. A court may award this bad-faith penalty whenever the facts warrant it, even if the tenant did not specifically request that relief. In any action under this statute, the landlord bears the burden of proving the reasonableness of amounts claimed against the deposit, or the landlord's authority to demand additional security. An action to recover a wrongfully retained deposit — including both actual and statutory damages — may be brought in small claims court if the total claimed falls within that court's jurisdictional dollar limit.
clauses.gap: "Bad faith" is not defined by a fixed statutory checklist here; it is a standard applied to the facts of each case, and a landlord's good-faith interpretation of what may be deducted, or a good-faith accounting error, is not automatically bad faith. This is one state's statutory remedy; the amount, structure, and even the existence of a bad-faith deposit-retention penalty vary by state, and this document addresses California's statewide statute only, not any city or county ordinance. All citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (Civil Code § 1950.5) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, the bad-faith retention penalty
citations.quote: The bad faith claim or retention by a landlord or the landlord's successors in interest of the security or any portion thereof in violation of this section, or the bad faith demand of replacement of security in violation of subdivision (k), may subject the landlord or the landlord's successors in interest to statutory damages of up to twice the amount of the security, in addition to actual damages. The court may award damages for bad faith whenever the facts warrant that award, regardless of whether the injured party has specifically requested relief. In an action under this section, the landlord or the landlord's successors in interest shall have the burden of proof as to the reasonableness of the amounts claimed or the authority pursuant to this section to demand additional security deposits.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, forfeiture of the entire deposit for bad-faith itemization noncompliance
citations.quote: The landlord shall not be entitled to claim any amount of the security if the landlord, in bad faith, fails to comply with this subdivision.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, small claims court jurisdiction over these damages
citations.quote: An action under this section may be maintained in small claims court if the damages claimed, whether actual, statutory, or both, are within the jurisdictional amount allowed by Section 116.220 or 116.221 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

clauses.title: Interest on the Deposit: Not Required by This Statute
clauses.body: California's security-deposit statute — the same statute that sets the deposit cap, the permitted uses, the 21-day return deadline, and the bad-faith penalty described elsewhere in this document — contains no provision requiring a landlord to pay interest on a tenant's security deposit while it is held. Its only references to the word "interest" anywhere in the statute concern a landlord's "interest in the premises" (ownership) and a landlord's "successor in interest" on a sale or transfer of the property — an unrelated legal use of the same word, not a security-deposit interest-payment obligation.
clauses.gap: This is a negative finding based on direct review of the current, complete text of California Civil Code section 1950.5 (the statute governing residential security deposits statewide) — not a claim that no California jurisdiction anywhere requires deposit interest. A number of California cities and counties with local rent-control or tenant-protection ordinances (San Francisco and Berkeley are commonly cited examples) separately require a landlord to pay tenants interest on a held security deposit, sometimes annually, under those local ordinances — but that obligation comes from municipal or county law, not from the statewide Civil Code section on which this document is based, and this document does not track any city's or county's local ordinance. Deposit-interest requirements also vary by state at the state level; some states require it and California's statewide rule does not. This is a single statutory citation confirming the absence of an interest-payment provision in the operative, currently amended text of the section; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, the full definitional/permitted-use provision, containing no interest obligation
citations.quote: As used in this section, "security" means any payment, fee, deposit, or charge, including, but not limited to, any payment, fee, deposit, or charge, except as provided in Section 1950.6, that is imposed at the beginning of the tenancy to be used to reimburse the landlord for costs associated with processing a new tenant or that is imposed as an advance payment of rent, used or to be used for any purpose, including, but not limited to, any of the following: (1) The compensation of a landlord for a tenant's default in the payment of rent. (2) The repair of damages to the premises, exclusive of ordinary wear and tear, caused by the tenant or by a guest or licensee of the tenant. (3) The cleaning of the premises upon termination of the tenancy necessary to return the unit to the same level of cleanliness it was in at the inception of the tenancy. (4) To remedy future defaults by the tenant in any obligation under the rental agreement to restore, replace, or return personal property or appurtenances, exclusive of ordinary wear and tear, if the security deposit is authorized to be applied thereto by the rental agreement.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, confirming the currently operative, fully reviewed version of the section
citations.quote: (Amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 340, Sec. 1. (AB 414) Effective January 1, 2026.)
