citations.cite: California Revenue and Taxation Code, interspousal transfers excluded from "change in ownership"
citations.quote: Notwithstanding any other provision in this chapter, a change of ownership shall not include any interspousal transfer, including, but not limited to: (a) Transfers to a trustee for the beneficial use of a spouse, or the surviving spouse of a deceased transferor, or by a trustee of such a trust to the spouse of the trustor, (b) Transfers which take effect upon the death of a spouse, (c) Transfers to a spouse or former spouse in connection with a property settlement agreement or decree of dissolution of a marriage or legal separation, or (d) The creation, transfer, or termination, solely between spouses, of any coowner’s interest. (e) The distribution of a legal entity’s property to a spouse or former spouse in exchange for the interest of such spouse in the legal entity in connection with a property settlement agreement or a decree of dissolution of a marriage or legal separation.

clauses.title: County Documentary Transfer Tax and Common Exemptions
clauses.body: California law authorizes — it does not itself directly impose — a county documentary transfer tax on a deed by which real property is granted, assigned, transferred, or otherwise conveyed, when the consideration or value of the interest conveyed exceeds $100. A county that adopts the tax by ordinance may charge $0.55 per $500 (or fractional part) of that consideration or value; a city within that county may separately adopt, by its own ordinance, up to half that rate on the same transfer. Two exemptions commonly relevant to a quitclaim deed exist in the statute: a deed that divides or allocates community, quasi-community, or quasi-marital property between spouses under, or in contemplation of, a dissolution or legal-separation judgment is exempt if the deed includes a written recital, signed by either spouse, stating that it is entitled to the exemption; and a deed made as an inter vivos gift, or by reason of death — including a transfer outright to, or in trust for the benefit of, any person or entity — is exempt as well.
clauses.gap: This states three genuinely separate sections of California's Documentary Transfer Tax Act — § 11911 (the tax itself), § 11927 (the marital-dissolution exemption), and § 11930 (the gift exemption) — treated here as three independent sources. This is not a complete list of every exemption in that Act; other exemptions exist for transaction types (for example, certain entity reorganizations and refinancings) not addressed here, and this clause does not determine whether a particular transfer, on its own facts, actually qualifies for either exemption described. Importantly, this statute is only the statewide/county documentary transfer tax framework: many California cities impose their own additional documentary transfer tax, and for some charter cities that additional tax has been adopted by voter initiative at rates and under authority that go beyond the half-of-the-county-rate structure that § 11911(b) itself describes for a general-law city. This document addresses the statewide/county documentary transfer tax framework only, not any particular city's additional tax, and is not a claim about which state's transfer-tax law applies to a given transfer.

citations.cite: California Revenue and Taxation Code, county (and city) documentary transfer tax
citations.quote: (a) The board of supervisors of any county or city and county, by an ordinance adopted pursuant to this part, may impose, on each deed, instrument, or writing by which any lands, tenements, or other realty sold within the county shall be granted, assigned, transferred, or otherwise conveyed to, or vested in, the purchaser or purchasers, or any other person or persons, by his or their direction, when the consideration or value of the interest or property conveyed (exclusive of the value of any lien or encumbrance remaining thereon at the time of sale) exceeds one hundred dollars ($100) a tax at the rate of fifty-five cents ($0.55) for each five hundred dollars ($500) or fractional part thereof. (b) The legislative body of any city which is within a county which has imposed a tax pursuant to subdivision (a) may, by an ordinance adopted pursuant to this part, impose, on each deed, instrument, or writing by which any lands, tenements, or other realty sold within the city shall be granted, assigned, transferred, or otherwise conveyed to, or vested in, the purchaser or purchasers, or any other person or persons, by his or their direction, when the consideration or value of the interest or property conveyed (exclusive of the value of any lien or encumbrance remaining thereon at the time of sale) exceeds one hundred dollars ($100), a tax at the rate of one-half the amount specified in subdivision (a) for each five hundred dollars ($500) or fractional part thereof. (c) A credit shall be allowed against the tax imposed by a county ordinance pursuant to subdivision (a) for the amount of any tax due to any city by reason of an ordinance adopted pursuant to subdivision (b). No credit shall be allowed against any county tax for a city tax which is not in conformity with this part.

citations.cite: California Revenue and Taxation Code, marital-dissolution exemption from the transfer tax
citations.quote: (a) Any tax imposed pursuant to this part shall not apply with respect to any deed, instrument, or other writing which purports to transfer, divide, or allocate community, quasi-community, or quasi-marital property assets between spouses for the purpose of effecting a division of community, quasi-community, or quasi-marital property which is required by a judgment decreeing a dissolution of the marriage or legal separation, by a judgment of nullity, or by any other judgment or order rendered pursuant to the Family Code, or by a written agreement between the spouses, executed in contemplation of any such judgment or order, whether or not the written agreement is incorporated as part of any of those judgments or orders. (b) In order to qualify for the exemption provided in subdivision (a), the deed, instrument, or other writing shall include a written recital, signed by either spouse, stating that the deed, instrument, or other writing is entitled to the exemption.

citations.cite: California Revenue and Taxation Code, gift exemption from the transfer tax
citations.quote: Any tax imposed pursuant to this part shall not apply to any deed, instrument, or other writing which purports to grant, assign, transfer, convey, divide, allocate, or vest lands, tenements, or realty, or any interest therein, if by reason of such inter vivos gift or by reason of the death of any person, such lands, tenements, realty, or interests therein are transferred outright to, or in trust for the benefit of, any person or entity.

clauses.title: Using This Deed Between Spouses: The Transmutation Requirement
clauses.body: When a quitclaim deed is used to add or remove a spouse from title to real property, California's Family Code imposes a formality on top of ordinary deed law. A change in the character of property between spouses — for example, from one spouse's separate property to community property, or from community property to one spouse's separate property — is called a transmutation. A transmutation of real property is not valid unless it is made in writing, by an express declaration, that is made, joined in, consented to, or accepted by the spouse whose interest in the property is adversely affected. Even a valid transmutation of real property is not effective as to third parties who lack notice of it unless the transmutation is recorded.
clauses.gap: This states California's own transmutation-formality rule for spouses; community-property and transmutation doctrine, and whether they apply at all, are not uniform among states, and this is not a claim about which state's law governs a particular married couple's transfer. § 852 does not itself define what makes a declaration "express" beyond its own text; California courts have addressed that question further in case law that this clause does not independently verify or cite, and that gap is disclosed rather than filled with an invented standard. The same statutory section separately exempts an interspousal gift of personal items such as clothing, wearing apparel, or jewelry that is not substantial in value — that exemption concerns personal property, not real property, and is not otherwise addressed here. This is a single statutory section (§ 852); no additional independent statutory source was located for the express-declaration requirement itself.

citations.cite: California Family Code, transmutation of real property between spouses
citations.quote: (a) A transmutation of real or personal property is not valid unless made in writing by an express declaration that is made, joined in, consented to, or accepted by the spouse whose interest in the property is adversely affected. (b) A transmutation of real property is not effective as to third parties without notice thereof unless recorded.

clauses.title: Grantor, Grantee, and Property Declaration
clauses.body: {{grantorName}} ("Grantor") remises, releases, and forever quitclaims to {{granteeName}} ("Grantee") all of Grantor's right, title, and interest in the real property located at {{propertyAddress}}. Grantor conveys only whatever interest Grantor actually holds in the property, if any, as of the date this deed is signed, and makes no covenant or warranty of any kind regarding the condition of title to that interest.

clauses.title: Legal Description Reference
clauses.body: The real property this deed transfers is more particularly described as follows, and this legal description controls if it differs from the street address given above: {{legalDescription}}. This deed also references Assessor's Parcel Number {{parcelNumber}}, provided for identification only.

clauses.title: Signature and Notarial Acknowledgment
clauses.body:
SIGNATURE AND DATE: {{grantorName}} signs and dates this deed below; the name should exactly match the name shown on the property's current title documents.

Signature of {{grantorName}}: _________________________ Date: _______________

ACKNOWLEDGMENT OF NOTARY: A notary public or other officer completing this certificate verifies only the identity of the individual who signed the document to which this certificate is attached, and not the truthfulness, accuracy, or validity of that document.

State of California ) County of _________________________ )

On _________________________ before me, _________________________ (here insert name and title of the officer), personally appeared _________________________, who proved to me on the basis of satisfactory evidence to be the person(s) whose name(s) is/are subscribed to the within instrument and acknowledged to me that they executed the same in their authorized capacity(ies), and that by their signature(s) on the instrument the person(s), or the entity upon behalf of which the person(s) acted, executed the instrument. I certify under PENALTY OF PERJURY under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing paragraph is true and correct.

WITNESS my hand and official seal.

Signature: _________________________ (Seal)

RECORDING: This deed transfers whatever interest {{grantorName}} has even if it is never recorded, but it is not recorded automatically upon signing. Recording is a separate step: presenting the signed, notarized deed to the county recorder in the county where the property is located, together with any required Preliminary Change of Ownership Report and any applicable documentary transfer tax.

clauses.title: The Statutory Basis for a Stand-Alone Instruction
clauses.body: An adult having capacity to make health care decisions may give an individual health care instruction directly, without executing a power of attorney for health care or naming any health care agent. {{patientName}}'s instruction may be oral or written, and may be limited to take effect only if a specified condition arises. California's Health Care Decisions Law treats this individual health care instruction as one of exactly two forms an advance health care directive can take — the other being a power of attorney for health care that appoints an agent — and a person may use either form alone, or combine both in one document.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a stand-alone instruction with no named agent is its own recognized category under this state's law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific instruction. Cal. Prob. Code § 4605 is the same definitional provision already cited in this project's Advance Health Care Directive document; it is cited again here only to show where a stand-alone instruction sits within that same two-part statutory structure, not as an independent new source for that structural point.

citations.cite: an adult may give an individual health care instruction without an agent
citations.quote: An adult having capacity may give an individual health care instruction. The individual instruction may be oral or written. The individual instruction may be limited to take effect only if a specified condition arises.

citations.cite: definition of advance health care directive as either component
citations.quote: "Advance health care directive" or "advance directive" means either an individual health care instruction or a power of attorney for health care.

clauses.title: What an Instruction Is For, and What It Can Address
clauses.body: The Legislature has found that an adult has the fundamental right to control decisions relating to their own health care, including the decision to have life-sustaining treatment withheld or withdrawn, and that prolonging the dying process for someone whose prognosis cannot be improved may cause needless pain and suffering without medical benefit. Consistent with that, an individual health care instruction can address the same broad range of health care decisions the statute recognizes: selection and discharge of health care providers and institutions; approval or disapproval of diagnostic tests, surgical procedures, and medication (including for mental health conditions); and directions to provide, withhold, or withdraw artificial nutrition and hydration and all other forms of health care, including cardiopulmonary resuscitation.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the Legislature's own stated purpose and of the actual breadth of subject matter an instruction can cover — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific instruction. § 4617 defines "health care decision" generally rather than "individual health care instruction" specifically; it is used here because an instruction operates by directing decisions within that same defined scope.

citations.cite: legislative findings on the right to refuse life-sustaining treatment
citations.quote: (a) In recognition of the dignity and privacy a person has a right to expect, the law recognizes that an adult has the fundamental right to control the decisions relating to his or her own health care, including the decision to have life-sustaining treatment withheld or withdrawn. (b) Modern medical technology has made possible the artificial prolongation of human life beyond natural limits. In the interest of protecting individual autonomy, this prolongation of the process of dying for a person for whom continued health care does not improve the prognosis for recovery may violate patient dignity and cause unnecessary pain and suffering, while providing nothing medically necessary or beneficial to the person.

citations.cite: the defined scope of health care decisions an instruction can address
citations.quote: "Health care decision" means a decision made by a patient or the patient's agent, conservator, or surrogate, regarding the patient's health care, including the following: (1) Selection and discharge of health care providers and institutions. (2) Approval or disapproval of diagnostic tests, surgical procedures, and programs of medication, including mental health conditions. (3) Directions to provide, withhold, or withdraw artificial nutrition and hydration and all other forms of health care, including cardiopulmonary resuscitation.

clauses.title: How This Differs From an AHCD With an Agent: No One Interprets It, a Provider Must Follow It Directly
clauses.body: Unlike a power of attorney for health care, an individual health care instruction does not appoint anyone to interpret it or to act on {{patientName}}'s behalf. That absence of an agent does not weaken the instruction: a health care provider or health care institution treating {{patientName}} must comply directly with {{patientName}}'s individual health care instruction, and — separately, if someone is then authorized to make health care decisions for {{patientName}}, such as an agent, surrogate, or conservator — must also comply with that person's reasonable interpretation of the instruction. The instruction is binding on its own; a named agent is not required to make it enforceable.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how an instruction operates without a named agent — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific instruction. The remainder of this compliance duty — its conscience-based and medically-ineffective-treatment exceptions, and the provider's notify-and-transfer obligation when it declines — is the identical duty already fully covered by this project's Advance Health Care Directive document (Cal. Prob. Code §§ 4734-4736); it is not re-derived here.

citations.cite: contrast: a power of attorney for health care requires executing an agent-appointment instrument
citations.quote: An adult having capacity may execute a power of attorney for health care, as provided in Article 2 (commencing with Section 4680). The power of attorney for health care may authorize the agent to make health care decisions and may also include individual health care instructions.

citations.cite: a provider's duty to comply with the instruction itself, independent of any interpreter
citations.quote: Except as provided in Sections 4734 and 4735, a health care provider or health care institution providing care to a patient shall do the following: (a) Comply with an individual health care instruction of the patient and with a reasonable interpretation of that instruction made by a person then authorized to make health care decisions for the patient.

clauses.title: Oral Instructions Need No Formality; Written Ones Follow the Same Rules as Any Written Directive
clauses.body: An individual health care instruction may be given orally, with no signing, dating, witnessing, or notarization of any kind. If {{patientName}} instead chooses to put the instruction in writing, that writing is a written advance health care directive and must meet the same legal-sufficiency requirements as any other one — it must state its execution date, be signed by {{patientName}} (or by another adult in {{patientName}}'s presence and at {{patientName}}'s direction), and be either notarized or signed by two qualifying witnesses. Those execution and witness-disqualification rules are already covered by this project's Advance Health Care Directive document and are not repeated here; this document exists specifically for the oral-or-simple-written case where no agent is being named.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that an oral instruction requires no formality at all, in contrast to a written one — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific instruction. The written-form execution requirement cited here (§ 4673(a)) is the same rule already fully quoted in this project's ahcd_execution_requirements clause; it is cited again only to establish that it applies identically to a written individual instruction, and is not a new or independent finding about that rule's content.

citations.cite: an instruction may be oral or written
citations.quote: An adult having capacity may give an individual health care instruction. The individual instruction may be oral or written. The individual instruction may be limited to take effect only if a specified condition arises.

citations.cite: legal sufficiency requirements that apply once an instruction is put in writing
citations.quote: A written advance health care directive is legally sufficient if all of the following requirements are satisfied: (1) The advance directive contains the date of its execution. (2) The advance directive is signed either by the patient or in the patient's name by another adult in the patient's presence and at the patient's direction. (3) The advance directive is either acknowledged before a notary public or signed by at least two witnesses who satisfy the requirements of Sections 4674 and 4675.

clauses.title: Revoking This Instruction Is Always the Easier Standard
clauses.body: While having capacity, {{patientName}} may revoke this individual health care instruction, in whole or in part, at any time and in any manner that communicates an intent to revoke — no signed writing is required. Because this document names no agent, none of it is ever subject to the stricter signed-writing-or-personal-notice rule that California law reserves specifically for revoking an agent designation.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual, looser revocation standard that applies to an instruction with no agent to designate or un-designate — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific instruction. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 4695(b)); the stricter agent-revocation subsection, § 4695(a), is already covered by this project's ahcd_revocation clause and does not apply to this document because it names no agent.

citations.cite: the looser revocation method for anything other than an agent designation
citations.quote: A patient having capacity may revoke all or part of an advance health care directive, other than the designation of an agent, at any time and in any manner that communicates an intent to revoke.

clauses.title: Declaration
clauses.body: I, {{patientName}}, being an adult of sound mind, give this individual health care instruction to make known my wishes regarding my own health care. I am not naming an agent or granting anyone power of attorney for health care in this document. I revoke any prior individual health care instruction I have made that is inconsistent with this one.

clauses.title: My Instructions
clauses.body: Regarding treatment intended to prolong my life: {{lifeProlongingWishes}}. Regarding relief from pain or discomfort: {{painReliefWishes}}. Additional instructions regarding my physical or mental health care: {{additionalHealthCareWishes}}. This instruction takes effect {{effectiveCondition}}.

clauses.title: Signature (If in Writing)
clauses.body:
This instruction may be given orally and need not be signed at all. If it is put in writing, as here, it should be signed and dated, and either notarized or signed by two qualifying witnesses, in the same manner as any other written advance health care directive.

Signature of {{patientName}}: ☐ _________________________ Date: _______________

clauses.title: Formation by Filing
clauses.body: {{companyName}} comes into existence as a California limited liability company on the date the California Secretary of State files its articles of organization — not on the date any operating agreement is signed, and not on the date the business starts operating. Before that filing is accepted, {{companyName}} has no legal existence as an LLC.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, cited here to show that formation-by-filing (rather than formation-by-agreement) is how one real state actually structures LLC creation — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular company; LLC formation mechanics vary by state. All three quotes below come from subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 17702.01, so they are treated as one source, not three independent ones. One thing this research could not verify: California's general corporation-filing statute (Cal. Corp. Code § 110) lets a corporation's filed instrument specify a delayed effective date up to 90 days out, but § 110 sits in the General Corporation Law (Title 1) and its delayed-effective-date language is written in terms of 'a corporation,' not an LLC. The current text of the LLC-specific formation statute, § 17702.01(d), states flatly that the LLC 'is formed when the Secretary of State has filed the articles of organization,' with no comparable 'or a later specified date' language found in this section or the surrounding LLC-formation article. Anyone relying on a delayed-effective-date option for an LLC filing should not assume one exists based on the corporation statute alone.

citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, formation by organizers filing articles of organization
citations.quote: One or more persons may act as organizers to form a limited liability company by signing and delivering to the Secretary of State for filing articles of organization on a form prescribed by the Secretary of State.

citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, the moment of formation
citations.quote: A limited liability company is formed when the Secretary of State has filed the articles of organization.

citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, filing as conclusive proof of formation
citations.quote: Except in a proceeding by this state to dissolve a limited liability company, the filing of the articles of organization by the Secretary of State is conclusive proof that the organizer satisfied all conditions to the formation of a limited liability company.

clauses.title: Required Content of the Articles of Organization
clauses.body: California's articles-of-organization statute requires the filed document to state: a lawful-purpose statement; the LLC's name (which must independently comply with the state's LLC-naming statute); the street address of the LLC's initial principal office, plus a separate mailing address if it differs; and the name and street address of the LLC's initial agent for service of process (address omitted if the agent is a registered corporate agent). Two further statements are required only if they apply — that the LLC will be manager-managed, or that it will be managed by a single manager — meaning the statute's default, absent either statement, is a member-managed LLC.
clauses.gap: This is one state's list of required formation-document content, not a claim about what any other state's equivalent filing must contain — required content for an LLC's founding filing varies by state. This quote is drawn from Cal. Corp. Code § 17702.01(b), the same statutory section quoted in the sibling clause on when an LLC is formed; both clauses draw on subsections of one section, not two independent sources. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 17702.01(b)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, required content of the articles of organization
citations.quote: The articles of organization shall state all of the following: (1) A statement that the purpose of the limited liability company is to engage in any lawful act or activity for which a limited liability company may be organized under this title. (2) The name of the limited liability company, which shall comply with Section 17701.08. (3) The street address of the initial principal office and the mailing address of the limited liability company if different from the street address of the initial principal office. (4) The name and street address of the initial agent for service of process of the limited liability company who meets the qualifications specified in subdivision (c) of Section 17701.13. If a corporate agent is designated, only the name of the agent shall be set forth. (5) If the limited liability company is to be manager-managed, the articles of organization shall contain a statement to that effect. (6) If the limited liability company is to be managed by only one manager, the articles of organization shall contain a statement to that effect.

clauses.title: The LLC Name Requirement
clauses.body: Under California's LLC-naming statute, an LLC's name must contain the words "limited liability company" or the abbreviation "LLC" or "L.L.C." (with "limited" shortenable to "Ltd." and "company" to "Co."). The same statute bars an LLC's name from including the words "bank," "trust," "trustee," "incorporated," "inc.," "corporation," or "corp.," and from including "insurer," "insurance company," or other words suggesting the business of issuing insurance policies.
clauses.gap: This is one state's naming statute, not a claim about naming rules in any other state — restricted words and required designators for an LLC name vary by state. Both quotes below come from subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.08, so they are one source, not two. One correction worth flagging: a commonly repeated assumption is that words like "city" are on this restricted list alongside "bank" and "corporation." The current, verified text of § 17701.08(e) does not include "city" or any municipal-sounding term among the restricted words — the restricted list here is limited to the banking/trust/insurance/corporate terms quoted above. This section also separately requires (in a subsection not quoted here, § 17701.08(b)) that a name be distinguishable in the Secretary of State's records from other registered entity names and not be likely to mislead the public, which is a separate, discretionary determination made by the Secretary of State rather than a fixed word list.

citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, required name designator
citations.quote: The name of a limited liability company shall contain the words "limited liability company," or the abbreviation "L.L.C." or "LLC." "Limited" may be abbreviated as "Ltd.," and "company" may be abbreviated as "Co."

citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, restricted words in an LLC name
citations.quote: The name shall not include the words "bank," "trust," "trustee," "incorporated," "inc.," "corporation," or "corp." and shall not include the words "insurer" or "insurance company" or any other words suggesting that it is in the business of issuing policies of insurance and assuming insurance risks.

clauses.title: Agent for Service of Process
clauses.body: California requires every LLC to continuously maintain, within the state, both an office and an agent for service of process. That agent must be either an individual who resides in California or a corporation qualified under state law to act as a registered corporate agent (in which case only the agent's name, not its address, is stated in the filing). If a designated agent resigns without being replaced, or cannot be located with reasonable diligence at its listed address, a court may order that the LLC instead be served by delivering process to the Secretary of State's office, with service deemed complete ten days after that delivery.
clauses.gap: This is one state's agent-for-service-of-process requirement, not a claim about what any other state requires — whether an LLC must maintain an in-state agent at all, and who may serve as one, varies by state. The first two quotes come from subsections of the same section, Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.13, and are treated as one source; the third quote, describing what happens when no agent can be found, comes from a separate section, Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.16, and is an independently verified source.

citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, duty to maintain an office and agent
citations.quote: A limited liability company shall designate and continuously maintain in this state both of the following: (1) An office, which need not be a place of its activity in this state. (2) An agent for service of process.

citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, who may serve as agent for service of process
citations.quote: An agent for service of process of a limited liability company or foreign limited liability company shall be an individual who is a resident of this state or a corporation that has complied with Section 1505 and whose capacity to act as an agent has not terminated. If a limited liability company or foreign limited liability company designates a corporation as its agent for service of process in an instrument filed with the Secretary of State, no address for that agent for service of process shall be set forth in that instrument.

citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, service on the Secretary of State when the agent cannot be found
citations.quote: If an agent for service of process has resigned and has not been replaced or if the designated agent cannot with reasonable diligence be found at the address designated for personal delivery of the process, and it is shown by affidavit to the satisfaction of the court that process against a limited liability company or foreign limited liability company cannot be served with reasonable diligence upon the designated agent by hand in the manner provided in Section 415.10, subdivision (a) of Section 415.20, or subdivision (a) of Section 415.30 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the court may make an order that the service shall be made upon a domestic limited liability company or upon a registered foreign limited liability company by delivering by hand to the Secretary of State, or to any person employed in the Secretary of State's office in the capacity of assistant or deputy, one copy of the process for each defendant to be served, together with a copy of the order authorizing the service. Service in this manner shall be deemed complete on the 10th day after delivery of the process to the Secretary of State.

clauses.title: The Follow-Up Statement of Information
clauses.body: Filing articles of organization does not end an LLC's filing obligations to the state. California requires every LLC to file an initial statement of information with the Secretary of State within 90 days after its articles of organization are filed, and then again every two years during the LLC's assigned filing period thereafter (or, if nothing has changed, to certify that no changes have occurred in lieu of refiling). The statement must report the LLC's name and Secretary of State file number, the name and street address of its current agent for service of process, its principal and mailing office addresses, the names and addresses of its managers (or, if it has none, its members), the general type of business it conducts, and a disclosure of whether any manager or member has an outstanding, non-appealable wage-order or Labor Code judgment against them.
clauses.gap: This is one state's periodic-reporting requirement for LLCs, not a claim about what any other state requires after formation — whether a follow-up report is required at all, and how often, varies by state. Both quotes below are subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 17702.09, and are treated as one source. This section notes it became operative in 2022 (or earlier upon a state IT-system certification); it has since been amended again, most recently effective January 1, 2023, so its current text is what is quoted here.

citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, initial and biennial statement of information
citations.quote: Every limited liability company and every foreign limited liability company registered to transact intrastate business in this state shall deliver to the Secretary of State for filing within 90 days after the filing of its original articles of organization or registering to transact intrastate business and biennially thereafter during the applicable filing period, on a form prescribed by the Secretary of State, a statement of information containing: (1) The name of the limited liability company and the Secretary of State's file number... (2) The name and street address of the agent in this state for service of process required to be maintained pursuant to Section 17701.13. If a corporate agent is designated, only the name of the agent shall be set forth. (3) The street address of its principal office... (4) The mailing address of the limited liability company or foreign limited liability company, if different from the street address of its principal office... (5) The name and complete business or residence addresses of any manager or managers and the chief executive officer, if any, appointed or elected in accordance with the articles of organization or operating agreement or, if no manager has been so elected or appointed, the name and business or residence address of each member. (6) If the limited liability company or foreign limited liability company chooses to receive renewal notices and any other notifications from the Secretary of State by electronic mail instead of by United States mail, the limited liability company or foreign limited liability company shall include a valid electronic mail address... (7) The general type of business that constitutes the principal business activity of the limited liability company or foreign limited liability company, such as, for example, manufacturer of aircraft, wholesale liquor distributor, or retail department store. (8) ...a statement indicating whether any manager [or member] has an outstanding final judgment issued by the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement or a court of law, for which no appeal therefrom is pending, for the violation of any wage order or provision of the Labor Code...

citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, how the two-year filing period is measured
citations.quote: For purposes of this section, the applicable filing period for a limited liability company shall be the calendar month during which its original articles of organization was filed or, in the case of a foreign limited liability company, the month during which its application for registration was filed, and the immediately preceding five calendar months. The Secretary of State shall provide a notice to each limited liability company or foreign limited liability company to comply with this section approximately three months prior to the close of the applicable filing period... The failure of the limited liability company or foreign limited liability company to receive the notice shall not exempt the limited liability company or foreign limited liability company from complying with this section.

clauses.title: The Annual LLC Tax
clauses.body: Filing articles of organization also triggers a state tax obligation separate from the Secretary of State's filing fee. California's Revenue and Taxation Code requires every LLC doing business in the state — and, independently, every LLC whose articles of organization have been accepted by the Secretary of State, whether or not it is yet doing business — to pay an annual tax in the amount set as the state's minimum franchise tax, currently eight hundred dollars ($800), due by the 15th day of the fourth month of the taxable year. That obligation continues for each taxable year, or part of one, until a certificate of dissolution or cancellation is filed with the Secretary of State.
clauses.gap: This is one state's minimum annual LLC tax, not a claim about what any other state charges — whether a state imposes a flat annual LLC tax at all, and in what amount, varies by state. The first two quotes below are subsections of the same section, Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 17941, and are one source; the $800 dollar figure itself is set in a separate section, Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23153(d)(1) (written for corporations generally but cross-referenced by § 17941(a) to set the LLC tax amount), and is an independently verified source. On the first-year exemption specifically: a temporary waiver did exist, but it applied only to LLCs that organized or registered with the Secretary of State on or after January 1, 2021 and before January 1, 2024 — that window has closed, so an LLC newly formed today would not fall within it. Separately, and more recently, the same statute (as amended by Stats. 2026, Ch. 85 (SB 180), effective July 13, 2026) now provides that for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2027 and before January 1, 2030, LLCs required to file a return under a specific cross-referenced provision (Rev. & Tax. Code § 18633.5) pay a reduced $400 tax for their first taxable year instead of the full $800 — a different, narrower provision than the earlier 2021-2023 exemption, tied to taxable years beginning in 2027-2029 rather than to a company's formation date, and not yet operative as of this verification date. This research did not independently trace § 18633.5 to confirm exactly which LLCs that reduced-rate provision reaches.

citations.cite: Tax and Fees on Limited Liability Companies, the annual tax for doing business in the state
citations.quote: Except as provided in subdivision (g), for each taxable year beginning on or after January 1, 1997, a limited liability company doing business in this state (as defined in Section 23101) shall pay annually to this state a tax for the privilege of doing business in this state in an amount equal to the applicable amount specified in subdivision (d) of Section 23153 for the taxable year.

citations.cite: Tax and Fees on Limited Liability Companies, the tax on filing (independent of doing business) and the now-expired 2021-2023 first-year exemption
citations.quote: In addition to any limited liability company that is doing business in this state and is therefore subject to the tax imposed by subdivision (a), for each taxable year beginning on or after January 1, 1997, a limited liability company shall pay annually the tax prescribed in subdivision (a) if articles of organization have been accepted, or a certificate of registration has been issued, by the office of the Secretary of State. The tax shall be paid for each taxable year, or part thereof, until a certificate of cancellation of registration or of articles of organization is filed on behalf of the limited liability company with the office of the Secretary of State. ... Every limited liability company doing business in this state as described in subdivision (a) that organizes or registers with the Secretary of the State pursuant to subdivision (b) on or after January 1, 2021, and before January 1, 2024, shall not be subject to the tax imposed under this section for its first taxable year.

citations.cite: The Corporation Franchise Tax, the $800 minimum franchise tax amount cross-referenced for LLCs
citations.quote: Except as provided in paragraph (2), paragraph (1) of subdivision (f) of Section 23151, paragraph (1) of subdivision (f) of Section 23181, and paragraph (1) of subdivision (c) of Section 23183, corporations subject to the minimum franchise tax shall pay annually to the state a minimum franchise tax of eight hundred dollars ($800).

clauses.title: Articles of Organization Declaration
clauses.body: The name of the limited liability company is {{companyName}}. The purpose of {{companyName}} is to engage in any lawful act or activity for which a limited liability company may be organized under the California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act. {{companyName}} will be {{managementStructure}}.

clauses.title: Agent for Service of Process Designation
clauses.body: The name of {{companyName}}'s initial agent for service of process in California is {{agentName}}. The agent's street address in California is {{agentAddress}}.

clauses.title: Organizer Signature
Residential-Only Statutes Don't Apply Here
clauses.body: California's residential security deposit statute, its statewide just-cause-for-termination rule, and its statewide rent-increase cap each apply only to residential tenancies, not to a commercial lease. Civil Code § 1950.5, the security deposit statute, states that it "applies to security for a rental agreement for residential property that is used as the dwelling of the tenant." Civil Code §§ 1946.2 (the just-cause termination rule) and 1947.12 (the rent-increase cap) each define their own scope as "residential real property," which both statutes define identically as "any dwelling or unit that is intended for human habitation." None of these three statutes contains language reaching a commercial tenancy.
clauses.gap: This document doesn't restate the security-deposit cap, the just-cause termination requirements, or the rent-increase cap found elsewhere in California law, because none of them govern a commercial lease by their own terms — a landlord and tenant negotiating a commercial lease are working from a different, thinner statutory baseline than a residential landlord and tenant. This is one state's statutes; some other states regulate commercial security deposits, commercial eviction notice, or commercial rent increases even though California generally does not for those specific protections (see the separate clauses on security deposits and notice elsewhere in this document for the commercial-specific rules that do exist). Two of the three citations below (§§ 1946.2 and 1947.12) happen to use identical definitional language for "residential real property," but they are independent, separately enacted and amended sections of the code, not subsections of one statute.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, scope of the residential security deposit statute
citations.quote: This section applies to security for a rental agreement for residential property that is used as the dwelling of the tenant.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, scope of the statewide just-cause statute
citations.quote: "Residential real property" means any dwelling or unit that is intended for human habitation, including any dwelling or unit in a mobilehome park.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, scope of the statewide rent-cap statute
citations.quote: "Residential real property" means any dwelling or unit that is intended for human habitation, including any dwelling or unit in a mobilehome park.

clauses.title: No Implied Warranty of Habitability for Commercial Space
clauses.body: California's implied warranty of habitability — the doctrine requiring a landlord to keep leased space fit for occupation — was recognized by the California Supreme Court specifically for residential leases, not commercial ones. Consistent with that, the statutory checklist defining what "habitable" specifically requires (Civil Code § 1941.1) is written in terms of a "dwelling," and the companion statute making the habitability duty non-waivable (Civil Code § 1942.1) is written in terms of "a lessee of a dwelling." Neither statute's text extends to commercial premises.
clauses.gap: A commercial tenant can't point to a defined statutory habitability checklist the way a residential tenant can. What a commercial space needs to be fit for its intended use is left almost entirely to what the lease itself says — which is why a commercial lease typically carries its own detailed condition-of-premises, maintenance, and repair provisions; state law doesn't fill that gap the way it does for a residential unit. This is one state's case law and statutory scheme, current as of this document's research date; some other states extend habitability-type protections to commercial tenants in narrower circumstances (for example, for latent defects known to the landlord), and this document doesn't track any state but California.

citations.quote: each of these jurisdictions has discarded the old common law rule and has adopted an implied warranty of habitability for residential leases... we have determined that the Hinson court properly recognized a common law implied warranty of habitability in residential leases in California.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, the tenantability checklist is dwelling-specific
citations.quote: A dwelling shall be deemed untenantable for purposes of Section 1941 if it substantially lacks any of the following affirmative standard characteristics or is a residential unit described in Section 17920.3 or 17920.10 of the Health and Safety Code...

citations.cite: California Civil Code, the non-waiver rule is dwelling-specific
citations.quote: Any agreement by a lessee of a dwelling waiving or modifying his rights under Section 1941 or 1942 shall be void as contrary to public policy with respect to any condition which renders the premises untenantable, except that the lessor and the lessee may agree that the lessee shall undertake to improve, repair or maintain all or stipulated portions of the dwelling as part of the consideration for rental.

clauses.title: Commercial Security Deposits Are Regulated Differently, Not Left Unregulated
clauses.body: Commercial security deposits are governed by a separate, less protective statute than the residential one — Civil Code § 1950.7 — rather than being entirely unregulated. Section 1950.7 doesn't cap the amount a commercial landlord can charge as a deposit, and it doesn't require the itemized statement that Civil Code § 1950.5 requires for a residential deposit. But it does restrict what the deposit can be used for — unpaid rent, repairing tenant-caused damage, and cleaning at the end of the tenancy — and it does set return deadlines: if the landlord's only claim is for possible unpaid rent and the deposit (plus anything designated as last month's rent) is one month's rent or less, any unused balance must be returned within 30 days of the landlord regaining possession; if that rent-only deposit exceeds one month's rent, the excess over one month must be returned within two weeks, with the remainder returned or accounted for within 30 days; and if the landlord's claim includes damage repair or cleaning, any unused balance must be returned within 30 days. A landlord who retains a commercial deposit in bad faith is liable for the tenant's actual damages plus a statutory penalty of up to $200.
clauses.gap: This is worth stating precisely because it corrects a common assumption: California doesn't simply have no rule for commercial security deposits — it has a real statute, just a much thinner one than the residential statute. There is no deposit-amount cap, no photo-documentation duty, no pre-move-out inspection right, and the bad-faith penalty tops out at $200 rather than residential's up-to-double-the-deposit exposure. Because there's no statutory cap on amount, the deposit figure in a commercial lease is set entirely by negotiation. This is one state's statute; other states regulate commercial deposits differently, including some with no statute on the subject at all. All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1950.7) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, scope of the commercial deposit statute
citations.quote: Any payment or deposit of money the primary function of which is to secure the performance of a rental agreement for other than residential property or any part of the agreement, other than a payment or deposit, including an advance payment of rent, made to secure the execution of a rental agreement, shall be governed by the provisions of this section. With respect to residential property, the provisions of Section 1950.5 shall prevail.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, permitted deductions and return deadlines
citations.quote: The landlord may claim of the payment or deposit only those amounts as are reasonably necessary to remedy tenant defaults in the payment of rent, to repair damages to the premises caused by the tenant, or to clean the premises upon termination of the tenancy, if the payment or deposit is made for any or all of those specific purposes. (1) If the claim of the landlord upon the payment or deposit is only for defaults in the payment of rent and the security deposit equals no more than one month's rent plus a deposit amount clearly described as the payment of the last month's rent, then any remaining portion of the payment or deposit shall be returned to the tenant at a time as may be mutually agreed upon by landlord and tenant, but in no event later than 30 days from the date the landlord receives possession of the premises.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, bad-faith retention penalty
citations.quote: The bad faith retention by a landlord or transferee of a payment or deposit or any portion thereof, in violation of this section, may subject the landlord or the transferee to damages not to exceed two hundred dollars ($200), in addition to any actual damages.

clauses.title: CASp Inspection Status Disclosure
clauses.body: A commercial property owner or lessor must state on every lease form or rental agreement executed on or after January 1, 2017, whether the premises have undergone inspection by a Certified Access Specialist (CASp). If the premises have not been issued a CASp disability access inspection certificate confirming compliance, the lease must include this exact statutory disclosure: "A Certified Access Specialist (CASp) can inspect the subject premises and determine whether the subject premises comply with all of the applicable construction-related accessibility standards under state law. Although state law does not require a CASp inspection of the subject premises, the commercial property owner or lessor may not prohibit the lessee or tenant from obtaining a CASp inspection of the subject premises for the occupancy or potential occupancy of the lessee or tenant, if requested by the lessee or tenant. The parties shall mutually agree on the arrangements for the time and manner of the CASp inspection, the payment of the fee for the CASp inspection, and the cost of making any repairs necessary to correct violations of construction-related accessibility standards within the premises."
clauses.gap: This applies to "commercial property" as this specific statute defines it — property offered for rent to someone operating, or intending to operate, a place of public accommodation, or a facility the general public is invited to — so it's aimed squarely at retail and public-facing space; the statute doesn't itself say whether it reaches every kind of non-public commercial lease (e.g., a private warehouse with no public access), and this document doesn't resolve that line. Separate rules apply if the premises have already been inspected and no impacting alterations have happened since (the CASp report must be shared with a confidentiality agreement, and a 72-hour rescission right applies if it isn't shared at least 48 hours before signing) — this clause's quoted paragraph is specifically for the no-certificate case. This is one state's statute; this particular pre-lease accessibility disclosure requirement is distinctive to California, not a nationwide practice. All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1938) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, the disclosure obligation
citations.quote: A commercial property owner or lessor shall state on every lease form or rental agreement executed on or after January 1, 2017, whether or not the subject premises have undergone inspection by a Certified Access Specialist (CASp).

citations.cite: California Civil Code, the required disclosure paragraph
citations.quote: If the subject premises have not been issued a disability access inspection certificate, as described in subdivision (e) of Section 55.53, the commercial property owner or lessor shall state the following on the lease form or rental agreement: "A Certified Access Specialist (CASp) can inspect the subject premises and determine whether the subject premises comply with all of the applicable construction-related accessibility standards under state law. Although state law does not require a CASp inspection of the subject premises, the commercial property owner or lessor may not prohibit the lessee or tenant from obtaining a CASp inspection of the subject premises for the occupancy or potential occupancy of the lessee or tenant, if requested by the lessee or tenant. The parties shall mutually agree on the arrangements for the time and manner of the CASp inspection, the payment of the fee for the CASp inspection, and the cost of making any repairs necessary to correct violations of construction-related accessibility standards within the premises."

citations.cite: California Civil Code, definition of "commercial property" for this section
citations.quote: As used in this section, "commercial property" means property that is offered for rent or lease to persons operating, or intending to operate, a place of public accommodation as defined in Section 202 of Chapter 2 of Part 2 of Title 24 of the California Code of Regulations, or a facility to which the general public is invited, at those premises.

clauses.title: Tenant's Right to Request a CASp Inspection
clauses.body: Section 1938 doesn't just require a disclosure — it separately protects the tenant's ability to have the premises inspected. Even though state law doesn't require a CASp inspection, the statute states the landlord "may not prohibit the lessee or tenant from obtaining a CASp inspection of the subject premises for the occupancy or potential occupancy of the lessee or tenant, if requested by the lessee or tenant." The statute requires the parties to "mutually agree on the arrangements for the time and manner of the CASp inspection, the payment of the fee for the CASp inspection, and the cost of making any repairs necessary" — meaning the statute itself does not assign that cost to either party by default; it's left to negotiation. Separately, if a CASp inspection has already happened and turned up violations, the statute presumes the landlord bears the cost of fixing them, "unless otherwise mutually agreed upon by the commercial property owner or lessor and the lessee or tenant."
clauses.gap: The task of confirming "who bears the cost" of a tenant-requested inspection has an honest answer that cuts against a natural assumption: the statute does not say the tenant pays for it. It requires the landlord and tenant to mutually agree on the fee, the timing, and the manner of the inspection — cost-shifting isn't automatic in either direction under this statute. What the statute does presume by default is that the landlord bears the cost of fixing violations an inspection turns up, unless the parties agree otherwise. This is one state's statute. All citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1938) as the CASp disclosure clause elsewhere in this document; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, tenant's right to request an inspection and cost/time arrangements
citations.quote: the commercial property owner or lessor may not prohibit the lessee or tenant from obtaining a CASp inspection of the subject premises for the occupancy or potential occupancy of the lessee or tenant, if requested by the lessee or tenant. The parties shall mutually agree on the arrangements for the time and manner of the CASp inspection, the payment of the fee for the CASp inspection, and the cost of making any repairs necessary to correct violations of construction-related accessibility standards within the premises.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, default responsibility for repairs found in an existing CASp report
citations.quote: Making any repairs or modifications necessary to correct violations of construction-related accessibility standards that are noted in a CASp report is presumed to be the responsibility of the commercial property owner or lessor, unless otherwise mutually agreed upon by the commercial property owner or lessor and the lessee or tenant.

clauses.title: Notice to End a Commercial Tenancy
clauses.body: For a periodic (e.g., month-to-month) commercial tenancy with no fixed end date, Civil Code § 1946 sets a default notice period of 30 days from either party to terminate — the same general default statute that applies to any periodic tenancy of real property, residential or commercial, unless the parties agree in the lease to a shorter period (as little as seven days). A narrower statute, Civil Code § 1946.1, extends the longer, residential-style 60-day (or 30-day, for a tenancy under a year) notice period to a "qualified commercial tenant" specifically — defined as a tenant that is a microenterprise, a restaurant with fewer than 10 employees, or a nonprofit with fewer than 20 employees, that has given the landlord a required written self-attestation of that status. Outside that narrow category, an ordinary commercial tenant gets the 30-day default under § 1946, not the 60-day residential-style period. For ending a tenancy for cause — nonpayment of rent or a lease breach — the same unlawful detainer statute used for residential tenancies, Code of Civil Procedure § 1161, applies to commercial tenancies too: it requires three days' written notice (excluding judicial holidays) to pay rent or quit, or to cure a covenant breach or quit, before an unlawful detainer action can be filed, because § 1161 applies broadly to "a tenant of real property," not only a residential dwelling unit. California law even sets out a separate set of notice-service methods specifically for a "commercial tenant" under Code of Civil Procedure § 1162, confirming the legislature understands this statute to reach commercial tenancies directly.
clauses.gap: This describes the statutory floor, not the whole picture — a fixed-term commercial lease typically states its own notice-and-cure terms, and none of this analysis governs a fixed-term lease that simply expires by its own stated end date (though the lease may separately require notice of intent to renew or vacate). Whether a specific tenant actually qualifies as a "qualified commercial tenant" under § 1946.1 depends on facts (entity type, employee count, and whether the required written self-attestation was actually given) that this document doesn't evaluate. This is one state's statutes, current as of a January 1, 2025 amendment that extended § 1946.1 to qualified commercial tenants for the first time — notice requirements for ending a commercial tenancy vary significantly by state, and some states impose no statutory notice floor at all for a commercial periodic tenancy. Two of the citations below (§ 1946.1(b)-(c) and § 1946.1(k)(4)) are subsections of the same statutory section, as are two others (§ 1161(2) and § 1161(7)); together, the citations below draw from four independently enacted statutes — §§ 1946, 1946.1, 1161, and 1162 — not one source restated multiple times.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, default 30-day notice to end a periodic tenancy of real property
citations.quote: A hiring of real property, for a term not specified by the parties, is deemed to be renewed as stated in Section 1945, at the end of the term implied by law unless one of the parties gives written notice to the other of that party's intention to terminate the same, at least as long before the expiration thereof as the term of the hiring itself, not exceeding 30 days; provided, however, that as to tenancies from month to month either of the parties may terminate the same by giving at least 30 days' written notice thereof at any time and the rent shall be due and payable to and including the date of termination. It shall be competent for the parties to provide by an agreement at the time the tenancy is created that a notice of the intention to terminate the same may be given at any time not less than seven days before the expiration of the term thereof.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, extended 60/30-day notice for a qualified commercial tenant
citations.quote: An owner of a residential dwelling or commercial real property hired by a qualified commercial tenant giving notice pursuant to this section shall give notice at least 60 days prior to the proposed date of termination. A tenant giving notice pursuant to this section shall give notice for a period at least as long as the term of the periodic tenancy prior to the proposed date of termination... an owner of a residential dwelling or commercial real property hired by a qualified commercial tenant giving notice pursuant to this section shall give notice at least 30 days prior to the proposed date of termination if a tenant or resident has resided in the dwelling or occupied the property for less than one year.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, definition of "qualified commercial tenant"
citations.quote: "Qualified commercial tenant" means a tenant of commercial real property that meets both of the following requirements: (A) The tenant is a microenterprise, a restaurant with fewer than 10 employees, or a nonprofit organization with fewer than 20 employees. (B) (i) Subject to clause (ii), the tenant has provided the landlord, within the previous 12 months, a written notice that the tenant is a qualified commercial tenant and a self-attestation regarding the number of employees, at such time the protections under this section come into place.

citations.cite: Code of Civil Procedure, three-day pay-rent-or-quit notice
citations.quote: When the tenant continues in possession, in person or by subtenant, without the permission of the landlord, or the successor in estate of the landlord, if applicable, after default in the payment of rent, pursuant to the lease or agreement under which the property is held, and three days' notice, excluding Saturdays and Sundays and other judicial holidays, in writing, requiring its payment, stating the amount that is due... or possession of the property, shall have been served upon the tenant and if there is a subtenant in actual occupation of the premises, also upon the subtenant.

citations.cite: Code of Civil Procedure, this notice statute is not limited to dwellings
citations.quote: As used in this section, "tenant" includes any person who hires real property except those persons whose occupancy is described in subdivision (b) of Section 1940 of the Civil Code.

citations.cite: Code of Civil Procedure, separate service methods and definition for a commercial tenant
citations.quote: The notices required by Section 1161 may be served upon a commercial tenant by any of the following methods: (1) By delivering a copy to the tenant personally. (2) If he or she is absent from the commercial rental property, by leaving a copy with some person of suitable age and discretion at the property, and sending a copy through the mail addressed to the tenant at the address where the property is situated... For purposes of subdivision (b), "commercial tenant" means a person or entity that hires any real property in this state that is not a dwelling unit, as defined in subdivision (c) of Section 1940 of the Civil Code, or a mobilehome, as defined in Section 798.3 of the Civil Code.

clauses.title: Personal Guaranties Are General Contract Law, Not a Commercial-Lease-Specific Statute
clauses.body: California has no statute written specifically for a personal guaranty of a commercial lease. What applies instead is the general contract-law statute of frauds: Civil Code § 1624(a)(2) makes "a special promise to answer for the debt, default, or miscarriage of another" — which is what a personal guaranty of a tenant entity's lease obligations is — unenforceable "unless they, or some note or memorandum thereof, are in writing and subscribed by the party to be charged or by the party's agent." Separately, the lease itself, if for a term longer than one year, independently must be in writing under Civil Code § 1624(a)(3).
clauses.gap: This is an honest gap in the sense the task asked to check for: there is no commercial-lease-specific guaranty statute in California comparable to, say, the CASp disclosure requirement. A personal guaranty of a commercial lease is enforced, or not, under the same general statute-of-frauds and suretyship principles that apply to a personal guaranty of any other kind of debt or obligation — principles found in Civil Code § 1624 and in the general suretyship statutes (Civil Code §§ 2787 et seq.), which this document doesn't otherwise cover. This is one state's statute of frauds; every state has some version of a statute of frauds covering a promise to answer for another's debt, but the exact wording and exceptions vary. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1624) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, statute of frauds for a promise to answer for another's debt
citations.quote: The following contracts are invalid, unless they, or some note or memorandum thereof, are in writing and subscribed by the party to be charged or by the party's agent... (2) A special promise to answer for the debt, default, or miscarriage of another, except in the cases provided for in Section 2794.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, statute of frauds for a lease longer than one year
citations.quote: An agreement for the leasing for a longer period than one year, or for the sale of real property, or of an interest therein; such an agreement, if made by an agent of the party sought to be charged, is invalid, unless the authority of the agent is in writing, subscribed by the party sought to be charged.

clauses.title: Parties, Premises, and Rent
clauses.body: This is a commercial lease agreement between {{landlordName}} ("Landlord") and {{tenantName}} ("Tenant") for the commercial premises located at {{propertyAddress}}. The lease term runs from {{leaseStartDate}} to {{leaseEndDate}}. Tenant will pay Landlord base rent of ${{monthlyRent}} per month, due on the day of each month specified in this agreement, payable by the method specified in this agreement. This lease is for commercial, non-residential use of the premises only. It does not create a residential tenancy, and the statutory protections that apply specifically to residential tenancies under California law do not apply to it.

clauses.title: Use of Premises
clauses.body: Tenant may use the premises only for the following purpose(s): {{permittedUse}} (the "Permitted Use"), and for no other purpose without Landlord's prior written consent. Confirming that the Permitted Use complies with applicable zoning, building, health, safety, and accessibility requirements for the premises is Tenant's responsibility.

clauses.title: Signatures
clauses.body:
Signed:

Landlord: ☐ _________________________ Date: _______________

Tenant: ☐ _________________________ Date: _______________

Guarantor (if applicable): ☐ _________________________ Date: _______________

A personal guaranty of Tenant's obligations under this lease is a separate promise that California law requires to be set out in a signed writing of its own; an individual's signature on this lease in a representative capacity for a business-entity Tenant does not, by itself, create a personal guaranty of that entity's obligations.

clauses.title: The Settlor's Statutory Power to Modify a Revocable Trust
clauses.body: Once {{trustName}} exists as a trust revocable by {{settlorName}}, California's Probate Code gives {{settlorName}} an independent statutory power to modify it, separate from the power to revoke it outright. Unless {{trustName}}'s own instrument provides otherwise, {{settlorName}} may modify {{trustName}} by following the same procedure the Probate Code provides for revoking it.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual statutory basis for a settlor's power to modify a revocable trust -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. The statute's current text is a single sentence, and that sentence does not itself offer 'a signed writing delivered to the trustee' as one alternative among several, with an additional catch-all allowing modification by any method that shows clear and convincing evidence of the settlor's intent. That broader 'clear and convincing evidence of intent' standard appears in some other states' trust statutes and in the Restatement (Third) of Trusts, but was not found in the current text of California Probate Code section 15402 itself -- so this document does not attribute that language to section 15402. What the modification power actually incorporates is whatever procedure a separate statute sets out for revocation, quoted in a different clause of this document. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 15402); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15402 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the settlor's statutory power to modify a revocable trust
citations.quote: Unless the trust instrument provides otherwise, if a trust is revocable by the settlor, the settlor may modify the trust by the procedure for revocation.

clauses.title: The Procedure for Revocation, Incorporated by Reference for Modification
clauses.body: Because {{trustName}}'s modification power works 'by the procedure for revocation,' the specific procedure that power incorporates comes from a separate Probate Code section governing revocation. That section provides two routes: compliance with whatever revocation method {{trustName}}'s own instrument sets out, or -- if {{trustName}}'s instrument doesn't make its own method the exclusive one -- a writing, other than a will, signed by {{settlorName}} and delivered to {{trusteeName}} during {{settlorName}}'s lifetime.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual procedure California's modification statute incorporates by reference -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. This same statutory section, Probate Code section 15401, is also the source for a separate clause of this document addressing a trust with more than one settlor; that clause quotes a different subdivision -- (b) -- of this same section, rather than an independent source, and this disclosure is made there as well. A further subdivision of this section, (e), also states that a trust created by an instrument executed before July 1, 1987 is governed by prior law rather than by this section; this document does not independently research what that prior law required.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15401(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the statutory methods of revocation, incorporated by section 15402 for modification
citations.quote: (a) A trust that is revocable by the settlor or any other person may be revoked in whole or in part by any of the following methods: (1) By compliance with any method of revocation provided in the trust instrument. (2) By a writing, other than a will, signed by the settlor or any other person holding the power of revocation and delivered to the trustee during the lifetime of the settlor or the person holding the power of revocation. If the trust instrument explicitly makes the method of revocation provided in the trust instrument the exclusive method of revocation, the trust may not be revoked pursuant to this paragraph.

clauses.title: When the Trust Instrument Makes Its Own Amendment Method Exclusive
clauses.body: If {{trustName}}'s own instrument states, in explicit terms, that its stated amendment or revocation method is the exclusive method, then the fallback method -- a signed writing delivered to {{trusteeName}} -- is not available; only the method the instrument itself specifies will do. A published California Court of Appeal decision, applying this same statutory framework, has summarized the rule this way: a trust may be revoked by complying with any method the trust instrument provides; if the instrument explicitly makes that method exclusive, the trust may be revoked only in that manner; if not, the trust may also be revoked by a writing, signed by the settlor and delivered to the trustee; and unless the trust provides otherwise, a trust may be modified by these same revocation procedures.
clauses.gap: This clause draws on the same Probate Code section 15401(a)(2) 'exclusive method' language already quoted in a separate clause of this document addressing the general revocation procedure, plus one independent source: a published California Court of Appeal decision, not a California Supreme Court decision. A search for a California Supreme Court decision squarely deciding whether a trust instrument's stated amendment method can be made exclusive did not turn up one on that specific question -- the most relevant California Supreme Court decision this search located, Donkin v. Donkin (2013) 58 Cal.4th 412, addresses a different question (how post-2010 no-contest-clause law applies to a trust amendment), not the exclusive-method question, so it is not cited here. The Court of Appeal decision quoted here, Huscher v. Wells Fargo Bank (2004) 121 Cal.App.4th 956, states the current-law rule in an overview passage, but the trust at issue in that case was created before July 1, 1987, so the court's actual holding turned on interpreting a prior Civil Code provision rather than on Probate Code sections 15401-15402 directly; the quoted passage is the court's own description of 'current law,' not the basis of its holding in that case. This is one state's case law and statute, used as real evidence -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust.

citations.case: Huscher v. Wells Fargo Bank (2004) 121 Cal.App.4th 956 (California Court of Appeal, Second Appellate District)
citations.cite: overview of the exclusive-method rule under Probate Code sections 15401-15402
citations.quote: Under current law, a trust may be revoked by complying with any method provided in the trust instrument. (Prob. Code, § 15401, subd. (a)(1).) If the trust explicitly makes that method exclusive, then it may be revoked only in that manner. If not, then the trust may also be revoked by a writing, other than a will, signed by the trustor and delivered to the trustee while the trustor is alive. (Prob. Code, § 15401, subd. (a)(2).) Unless the trust provides otherwise, the trust may be modified by the revocation procedures of Probate Code section 15401. (Prob. Code, § 15402.)

clauses.title: The Capacity Standard for Amending a Trust
clauses.body: The Probate Code sets a general legal-capacity standard that, by its own terms, applies to a person's capacity 'to execute trusts,' among other acts. That general standard applies 'except where otherwise provided by law' -- and the statute setting that general standard itself lists 'the statutory and decisional law of testamentary capacity' as an example of law that can displace it. A published California Court of Appeal decision has held that when a settlor's trust amendment, in its content and complexity, closely resembles a will or codicil, it is that lower, will-specific testamentary-capacity standard -- not the Probate Code's general capacity statute standing alone -- that a court should use to evaluate the settlor's capacity to make the amendment.
