clauses.title: California's Trade Secret Definition
clauses.body: Like the parties' own definition of confidential information in this agreement, California's Uniform Trade Secrets Act has its own, separate definition of "trade secret" that applies regardless of what this contract says. Under that statute, a trade secret is information that (1) derives independent economic value from not being generally known to others who could profit from it, and (2) is the subject of efforts reasonable under the circumstances to keep it secret. Both {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} can agree in this contract to treat a broader category of information as confidential than the statute would separately protect as a trade secret — the two are not the same thing, and this agreement's confidentiality promises don't depend on the disclosed information actually meeting the statutory test.
clauses.gap: This is California's statute, used as real evidence of the state's own trade-secret definition — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs this agreement or any dispute under it. The wording differs somewhat from the federal Defend Trade Secrets Act's definition, which uses 'reasonable measures' rather than 'efforts reasonable under the circumstances' and separately requires that the information not be 'readily ascertainable through proper means' — the practical difference between these formulations, if any, was not tested against case law in this research. No case law interpreting this specific California definition was checked here; the statute's own text is unambiguous about the two-element test, so the statute stands as the source without a corroborating case. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (§ 3426.1(d)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.cite: California Uniform Trade Secrets Act, definition of "trade secret"
citations.quote: “Trade secret” means information, including a formula, pattern, compilation, program, device, method, technique, or process, that: (1) Derives independent economic value, actual or potential, from not being generally known to the public or to other persons who can obtain economic value from its disclosure or use; and (2) Is the subject of efforts that are reasonable under the circumstances to maintain its secrecy.

clauses.title: This Contract's Confidentiality Duty Is Separate from Trade Secret Law
clauses.body: California's trade secret statute expressly does not take away or limit contractual confidentiality remedies, whether or not the information at issue would separately qualify as a trade secret. That means a breach of this agreement's confidentiality promises can be pursued as a contract claim on its own terms, without either {{party1Name}} or {{party2Name}} having to first show the disclosed information met the statutory trade-secret test. Separately, California's trade secret statute sets its own three-year discovery-rule deadline for bringing a trade-secret misappropriation lawsuit — but that deadline applies only to misappropriation claims under that statute. It does not set, extend, or limit how long this agreement's own confidentiality obligations last; that duration is whatever term the parties write into this contract.
clauses.gap: This is California's statute, used as real evidence of how that state's trade secret law relates to contract law — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs this agreement. No case law applying this displacement provision to a mutual non-disclosure agreement specifically was checked in this research; the statutory text is unambiguous on its own terms about preserving contractual remedies, so the statute stands as the source here without a corroborating case. Separately: outside of trade-secret misappropriation claims specifically, there is no special statutory deadline for suing over a plain breach of a confidentiality contract — an ordinary breach-of-contract claim would instead be governed by California's general statute of limitations for written contracts, which was not independently verified in this research and is not quoted here.

citations.cite: California Uniform Trade Secrets Act, effect on other remedies
citations.quote: This title does not affect (1) contractual remedies, whether or not based upon misappropriation of a trade secret, (2) other civil remedies that are not based upon misappropriation of a trade secret, or (3) criminal remedies, whether or not based upon misappropriation of a trade secret.

citations.cite: California Uniform Trade Secrets Act, statute of limitations for misappropriation
citations.quote: An action for misappropriation must be brought within three years after the misappropriation is discovered or by the exercise of reasonable diligence should have been discovered. For the purposes of this section, a continuing misappropriation constitutes a single claim.

clauses.title: Whether the Federal Whistleblower Notice Applies to a Company-to-Company Agreement
clauses.body: Federal law's whistleblower immunity notice requirement is written to apply to "any contract or agreement with an employee that governs the use of a trade secret or other confidential information," and the statute defines "employee," for purposes of that notice requirement only, to include "any individual performing work as a contractor or consultant for an employer." A mutual non-disclosure agreement between two business entities, where neither {{party1Name}}'s nor {{party2Name}}'s individual personnel is personally performing contractor or consultant work for the other side, sits outside that statutory language on its face — the notice mandate is framed around an individual doing work for an employer, not two companies exchanging information as counterparties. The same federal notice requirement is squarely triggered, by contrast, whenever one of the parties to a confidentiality agreement is an individual, sole proprietor, or independent contractor performing work for the other rather than a business entity dealing at arm's length.
clauses.gap: This clause cites two paragraphs of the same statutory subsection, 18 U.S.C. § 1833(b) — (b)(3)(A) and (b)(4); no additional independent source was found for either point beyond the statute's own text. This is the federal government's statute, used as real evidence of what the notice requirement's own text covers — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs this agreement. No case law was checked on how courts have resolved close cases at this boundary (for example, a sole proprietor doing business under a company name, or a company whose only "employee" is its own owner) — the statute's own text is unambiguous about the general rule, so it stands as the source here without a corroborating case. This is a scoping question only, distinct from the existing one-way NDA's whistleblower-notice clause: that clause already covers the immunity's substance, the notice-and-consequence rule, the policy-document alternative, and the anti-retaliation carve-out in full, and none of that is repeated here.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, Defend Trade Secrets Act, notice requirement
citations.quote: An employer shall provide notice of the immunity set forth in this subsection in any contract or agreement with an employee that governs the use of a trade secret or other confidential information.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, Defend Trade Secrets Act, definition of "employee" for the notice requirement
citations.quote: For purposes of this subsection, the term "employee" includes any individual performing work as a contractor or consultant for an employer.

clauses.title: Confidential Information, Defined Reciprocally
clauses.body: Either {{party1Name}} or {{party2Name}} may be the party disclosing information (the "Disclosing Party") or the party receiving it (the "Receiving Party") under this agreement, and that role can switch depending on which direction information is flowing at a given time. Each party's confidential information includes any business, technical, financial, or other information that party discloses to the other and marks or otherwise identifies as confidential, or that a reasonable person would understand to be confidential given its nature and the circumstances of disclosure. This definition and the protections that go with it apply equally regardless of which party is disclosing and which is receiving at that time.

clauses.title: Reciprocal Confidentiality Obligations
clauses.body: Each of {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} will keep the other's confidential information private, use it only for the purpose of {{purposeOfDisclosure}}, and take reasonable care to prevent anyone else from accessing it. These duties run in both directions on identical terms: whichever party is the Receiving Party at a given time owes the other the same obligations described here.

clauses.title: What This Mutual Agreement Doesn't Cover
clauses.body: This agreement doesn't restrict information that was already public, that the Receiving Party already knew before receiving it from the Disclosing Party, that the Receiving Party develops independently without using the Disclosing Party's confidential information, or that the Receiving Party is required to disclose by law — though the Receiving Party will tell the Disclosing Party first if legally able to. These exclusions apply the same way to {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}, whichever one is receiving information at the time.

clauses.title: Term, Survival, and Signatures
clauses.body:
This agreement's confidentiality obligations continue for {{confidentialityDuration}} from the date each piece of information is disclosed. That duration is a term the parties are setting for themselves in this contract, not a period fixed by statute.

Please sign below to indicate agreement to the terms above.

{{party1Name}}: _______________
Date: _______________

{{party2Name}}: _______________
Date: _______________

clauses.title: COBRA Qualifying Events
clauses.body: Federal law lists six specific events that can trigger a covered employee's or family member's right to elect continuation coverage under a group health plan: (1) the covered employee's death; (2) the covered employee's termination of employment (other than for gross misconduct) or a reduction in hours; (3) the covered employee's divorce or legal separation from their spouse; (4) the covered employee becoming entitled to Medicare; (5) a dependent child ceasing to be a dependent child under the plan's own terms; and (6) certain employer bankruptcy proceedings affecting retiree coverage. Any of these events that would otherwise cause a qualified beneficiary to lose coverage can be a "qualifying event" that starts the continuation-coverage process for {{employeeName}} and, where applicable, {{employeeName}}'s covered spouse and dependents.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of what the statute defines as a qualifying event nationally — not a claim that this particular company's plan is subject to COBRA or that this particular employee's own circumstances match one of these six categories. Whether a given termination was genuinely "for gross misconduct" (the one carve-out named in the statute for event (2)) is a fact-specific determination this clause does not make. This clause lists the statutory categories; it does not determine which one, if any, applies here. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 1163); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, definition of "qualifying event"
citations.quote: For purposes of this part, the term "qualifying event" means, with respect to any covered employee, any of the following events which, but for the continuation coverage required under this part, would result in the loss of coverage of a qualified beneficiary: (1) The death of the covered employee. (2) The termination (other than by reason of such employee's gross misconduct), or reduction of hours, of the covered employee's employment. (3) The divorce or legal separation of the covered employee from the employee's spouse. (4) The covered employee becoming entitled to benefits under title XVIII of the Social Security Act. (5) A dependent child ceasing to be a dependent child under the generally applicable requirements of the plan. (6) A proceeding in a case under title 11, commencing on or after July 1, 1986, with respect to the employer from whose employment the covered employee retired at any time.

clauses.title: COBRA Notice Timing Obligations
clauses.body: Federal law imposes a two-step notice chain once a qualifying event occurs. First, for a qualifying event like termination of employment, {{companyName}} (as employer) must notify the group health plan's administrator of the qualifying event within 30 days of the date of the event. Second, once the plan administrator has that notice, the administrator must in turn notify each qualified beneficiary — {{employeeName}} and, where applicable, {{employeeName}}'s covered spouse and dependents — of their continuation-coverage election rights within 14 days of the date the administrator was notified.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the two-step statutory notice chain — not a claim that this particular company is itself the plan administrator, that it has already given this notice, or that this particular plan is subject to COBRA at all. The statute states the 30-day and 14-day periods as two separate, sequential steps (employer to administrator, then administrator to beneficiary); it does not itself state a single combined "44 days" figure. A combined ~44-day outer bound is commonly described in U.S. Department of Labor guidance and regulations (29 C.F.R. § 2590.606-4) that synthesize these two statutory periods for the common case where the employer is also the plan administrator, but that combined figure was not independently verified against primary regulatory text for this clause and is not asserted here as a direct quotation of § 1166 itself — only the two statutory periods it draws from are quoted below. Both citations are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1166); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, COBRA employer notice to plan administrator
citations.quote: the employer of an employee under a plan must notify the administrator of a qualifying event described in paragraph (1), (2), (4), or (6) of section 1163 of this title within 30 days ... of the date of the qualifying event

citations.cite: U.S. Code, COBRA administrator notice to qualified beneficiaries
citations.quote: For purposes of subsection (a)(4), any notification shall be made within 14 days (or, in the case of a group health plan which is a multiemployer plan, such longer period of time as may be provided in the terms of the plan) of the date on which the administrator is notified under paragraph (2) or (3), whichever is applicable.

clauses.title: 60-Day COBRA Election Period
clauses.body: Federal law gives each qualified beneficiary an election period of at least 60 days to elect continuation coverage. That period begins no later than the date coverage would otherwise terminate because of the qualifying event, and ends no earlier than 60 days after the later of that termination date or the date the qualified beneficiary is sent the COBRA election notice. Coverage may not require payment of any premium before the day that is 45 days after the date the qualified beneficiary makes the initial election.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the minimum statutory election window and the minimum initial-payment grace period — not a claim about the specific dates that apply to this particular employee's own election, which depend on when the qualifying event occurred and when the election notice was actually sent. This clause states the general 60-day/45-day statutory minimums; it does not calculate the employee's actual election or first-payment deadline.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, COBRA election period
citations.quote: The term "election period" means the period which— (A) begins not later than the date on which coverage terminates under the plan by reason of a qualifying event, (B) is of at least 60 days' duration, and (C) ends not earlier than 60 days after the later of— (i) the date described in subparagraph (A), or (ii) in the case of any qualified beneficiary who receives notice under section 1166(4) of this title, the date of such notice.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, COBRA initial premium payment deadline
citations.quote: In no event may the plan require the payment of any premium before the day which is 45 days after the day on which the qualified beneficiary made the initial election for continuation coverage.

clauses.title: Scope and Maximum Duration of COBRA Continuation Coverage
clauses.body: Federal law requires that continuation coverage be identical to the coverage the plan provides to similarly situated active employees and their families who have not had a qualifying event; if the plan's coverage changes for that comparison group, it must change the same way for people on continuation coverage. For a qualifying event that is a termination of employment or reduction of hours, the coverage must last at least until 18 months after the qualifying event. For most other qualifying events (death, divorce or legal separation, Medicare entitlement, or loss of dependent-child status), the required period extends to at least 36 months after the qualifying event. If a second qualifying event occurs during an 18-month period that started with a termination or reduced-hours event, the maximum period can extend to 36 months from the original event.
clauses.gap: This is federal law (a single statutory section, 29 U.S.C. § 1162; no additional independent source was found for this), used as real evidence of the coverage-parity requirement and the general 18-month/36-month maximum-period framework — not a claim about what this particular company's specific plan actually covers or costs. The statute contains additional special rules not restated here in full (bankruptcy-related events, Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation recipients, a disability extension to 29 months, and a rule for Medicare entitlement followed by a later qualifying event); this clause states the general rule, not every extension scenario.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, COBRA coverage-parity requirement
citations.quote: The coverage must consist of coverage which, as of the time the coverage is being provided, is identical to the coverage provided under the plan to similarly situated beneficiaries under the plan with respect to whom a qualifying event has not occurred.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, COBRA maximum coverage periods
citations.quote: In the case of a qualifying event described in section 1163(2) of this title, except as provided in clause (ii), the date which is 18 months after the date of the qualifying event. ... If a qualifying event (other than a qualifying event described in section 1163(6) of this title) occurs during the 18 months after the date of a qualifying event described in section 1163(2) of this title, the date which is 36 months after the date of the qualifying event described in section 1163(2) of this title. ... In the case of a qualifying event not described in section 1163(2) or 1163(6) of this title, the date which is 36 months after the date of the qualifying event.

clauses.title: COBRA Premium — Up to 102% of Applicable Premium
clauses.body: A plan may charge a qualified beneficiary for continuation coverage, but federal law caps that charge at 102% of the plan's "applicable premium" — generally, the cost the plan would otherwise use for similarly situated active employees and their families, without regard to who pays it. Payment may be made in monthly installments if the qualified beneficiary elects that. A different, higher cap (150% instead of 102%) applies only to certain months of extended coverage tied to the statute's disability-extension rule, not to the general case.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, drawn from two different statutory sections that work together — the 102%-of-applicable-premium cap itself is stated in 29 U.S.C. § 1162(3)(A), while "applicable premium" is defined separately in 29 U.S.C. § 1164 — used as real evidence of the statutory premium ceiling, not a claim about what this particular company's plan actually charges or what this particular employee will actually be billed. Note for drafting accuracy: the 102% figure itself is not located in § 1164 (which only defines the underlying "applicable premium" cost figure); it is located in § 1162(3)(A), which caps what a plan may charge relative to that defined figure. This clause states the general premium cap; it does not address the separate 150%-of-applicable-premium rule that applies only during certain months of a disability extension.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, COBRA premium cap
citations.quote: The plan may require payment of a premium for any period of continuation coverage, except that such premium— (A) shall not exceed 102 percent of the applicable premium for such period, and (B) may, at the election of the payor, be made in monthly installments.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, definition of "applicable premium"
citations.quote: The term "applicable premium" means, with respect to any period of continuation coverage of qualified beneficiaries, the cost to the plan for such period of the coverage for similarly situated beneficiaries with respect to whom a qualifying event has not occurred (without regard to whether such cost is paid by the employer or employee).

clauses.title: COBRA's Employer-Size Threshold and Cal-COBRA
clauses.body: Federal COBRA continuation-coverage rules do not apply to every group health plan. They are excepted for any calendar year in which all employers maintaining the plan normally employed fewer than 20 employees on a typical business day during the preceding calendar year. Separately, California has its own state continuation-coverage law — the California Continuation Benefits Replacement Act, commonly called "Cal-COBRA" — enacted specifically to extend similar coverage rights to employees of smaller employers (with 2 to 19 eligible employees) who are not otherwise covered by federal COBRA.
clauses.gap: The federal-law statement above (fewer than 20 employees) is federal law, used as real evidence of COBRA's own small-employer exception — not a claim about this particular company's actual headcount or whether its plan is or is not subject to COBRA. Cal-COBRA is a genuinely distinct, separate state statutory scheme (California Health and Safety Code § 1366.20 et seq., part of the Knox-Keene Act framework, with a parallel scheme for insured plans in the Insurance Code) with its own eligibility rules, notice timelines, and maximum coverage periods that are not restated in this document, which addresses federal COBRA only. Whether Cal-COBRA (rather than, or in addition to, federal COBRA) applies to this particular company depends on facts — employer size, plan type, and whether the plan is insured or self-funded — that this clause does not resolve.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, COBRA small-employer exception
citations.quote: Subsection (a) shall not apply to any group health plan for any calendar year if all employers maintaining such plan normally employed fewer than 20 employees on a typical business day during the preceding calendar year.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 1366.20(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Health and Safety Code, Cal-COBRA
citations.quote: (a) This article shall be known as the California Continuation Benefits Replacement Act, or "Cal-COBRA." (b) It is the intent of the Legislature that continued access to health insurance coverage is provided to employees, and their dependents, of employers with 2 to 19 eligible employees who are not currently offered continuation coverage under the Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1985.

clauses.title: COBRA Election Notice Letter
clauses.body:
COBRA CONTINUATION COVERAGE ELECTION NOTICE

Date: {{noticeDate}}

To: {{employeeName}}

From: {{companyName}}, on behalf of the Plan Administrator of {{planName}}

Re: Your Right to Elect COBRA Continuation Coverage

This notice is to inform you of your rights under the federal law known as COBRA (the Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act) to continue your group health plan coverage.

1. Qualifying Event. On {{qualifyingEventDate}}, you experienced the following qualifying event: {{qualifyingEventType}}. This event resulted, or will result, in a loss of coverage under {{planName}}.

2. Who May Elect Coverage. You, and any covered spouse or dependent children who were covered under the plan immediately before the qualifying event, are each a "qualified beneficiary" and may independently elect continuation coverage.

3. Your Election Period. You have at least 60 days from the later of (a) the date coverage would otherwise end, or (b) the date of this notice, to elect continuation coverage. If you do not elect coverage within that period, your right to elect COBRA continuation coverage will end.

4. Cost of Coverage. If you elect continuation coverage, you may be required to pay up to 102% of the full cost of coverage. The estimated monthly premium is {{monthlyPremiumAmount}}. You are not required to make your first payment until 45 days after the date you elect coverage.

5. Duration of Coverage. Continuation coverage elected in connection with this qualifying event may last for up to {{maxCoverageMonths}} months, subject to the plan's terms and the statutory rules governing early termination, extension, and second qualifying events.

6. How to Elect. To elect continuation coverage, complete and return the attached election form to {{planAdministratorName}} at {{planAdministratorAddress}} by {{electionDeadline}}.

This notice summarizes your rights under the plan and applicable law. It is not a complete description of the plan or of COBRA, and it does not modify the plan's actual terms.

clauses.body:

I elect the following (check applicable):
[  ] I elect to continue coverage for myself.

[  ] I decline continuation coverage for myself and all listed qualified beneficiaries.

I understand that:

- Continuation coverage, once elected, is subject to the terms of {{planName}} and to applicable law, including the plan's right to terminate continuation coverage early for the reasons permitted by law (for example, non-payment of premium, the qualified beneficiary becoming covered under another group health plan, or the plan ceasing to provide group health coverage to any employee).

Signature: ______________________  Date: {{dateSigned}}

clauses.title: Scope of This Document and Distinction from Civil Harassment Orders
clauses.body: California Family Code section 6200 states that Division 10 of the Family Code -- sections 6200 through 6460 -- may be cited as the Domestic Violence Prevention Act (DVPA). Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6(w) states that the civil harassment restraining order statute does not apply to any action or proceeding covered by the DVPA. The DVPA governs a restraining order between people who have one of the specific relationships listed in Family Code section 6211 (for example spouses, cohabitants, dating partners, co-parents, or certain close relatives), while Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6 governs harassment between people who do not have such a relationship. This document is an informational description of the DVPA process under Family Code section 6200 et seq. It states what the statute provides; it does not itself grant, deny, or constitute a restraining order. Only a court, applying this statutory process to a specific petition, can issue a restraining order.
clauses.gap: This clause draws on two different, independently enacted California statutes -- Family Code section 6200 (the DVPA's short-title provision) and Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6(w) (the civil harassment statute's carve-out for DVPA-covered proceedings) -- rather than multiple subsections of a single section, so no single-section disclosure applies here. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California itself distinguishes its domestic violence restraining order process from its civil harassment restraining order process -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific petitioner's or respondent's relationship, or about whether an equivalent statutory distinction exists in any other state. Whether a specific relationship qualifies under Family Code section 6211 is a question of fact and law this clause does not resolve for any individual case.

citations.cite: the Domestic Violence Prevention Act's short title
citations.quote: This division may be cited as the Domestic Violence Prevention Act.

citations.cite: civil harassment does not cover DVPA-governed proceedings
citations.quote: This section does not apply to any action or proceeding covered by Title 1.6C (commencing with Section 1788) of Part 4 of Division 3 of the Civil Code or by Division 10 (commencing with Section 6200) of the Family Code. This section does not preclude a petitioner from using other existing civil remedies.

clauses.title: Who Qualifies for a DVPA Restraining Order
clauses.body: Family Code section 6211 limits DVPA protection to abuse committed against specific categories of people: a spouse or former spouse; a cohabitant or former cohabitant, as defined in Family Code section 6209; a person the respondent is having or has had a dating or engagement relationship with; a person with whom the respondent has had a child, where a parentage presumption applies; a child of a party, or a child who is the subject of a parentage action, where that presumption applies; and any other person related to the respondent by consanguinity or affinity within the second degree. Family Code section 6209 defines a "cohabitant" as a person who regularly resides in the household, and a "former cohabitant" as a person who formerly regularly resided in the household.
clauses.gap: Family Code section 6211's list and Family Code section 6209's definition are two different, independently added statutory sections, so no single-section disclosure applies here. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of which relationships California's DVPA covers -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific pair of people, or about whether an equivalent relationship-based eligibility list exists in any other state's domestic violence statute. Whether a specific relationship falls within one of these categories -- for example, what makes a residence "regular" for cohabitant status, or what counts as a qualifying dating relationship -- has been the subject of considerable case law not reviewed for this clause; this clause states only the statutory categories, not how courts have applied them to particular facts.

citations.cite: the statutory list of qualifying relationships
citations.quote: "Domestic violence" is abuse perpetrated against any of the following persons: (a) A spouse or former spouse. (b) A cohabitant or former cohabitant, as defined in Section 6209. (c) A person with whom the respondent is having or has had a dating or engagement relationship. (d) A person with whom the respondent has had a child, where the presumption applies that the male parent is the father of the child of the female parent under the Uniform Parentage Act... (e) A child of a party or a child who is the subject of an action under the Uniform Parentage Act, where the presumption applies that the male parent is the father of the child to be protected. (f) Any other person related by consanguinity or affinity within the second degree.

citations.cite: the definition of cohabitant and former cohabitant
citations.quote: "Cohabitant" means a person who regularly resides in the household. "Former cohabitant" means a person who formerly regularly resided in the household.

clauses.title: Statutory Definition of "Abuse" Under the DVPA
clauses.body: Family Code section 6203(a) defines "abuse," for purposes of the Domestic Violence Prevention Act, as any of the following: intentionally or recklessly causing or attempting to cause bodily injury; sexual assault; placing a person in reasonable apprehension of imminent serious bodily injury to that person or to another; or engaging in any behavior that has been or could be enjoined under Family Code section 6320. Section 6203(b) states that abuse is not limited to the actual infliction of physical injury or assault.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California currently defines "abuse" under its Domestic Violence Prevention Act -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific petitioner, respondent, or set of facts, and not a claim that another state's domestic violence statute defines abuse the same way. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 6203(a)-(b)); no additional independent source was found for this. Note for drafters: California's DVPA "abuse" definition is materially broader than a lay reading of the word -- it reaches conduct enjoinable under section 6320 (see the companion clause on disturbing the peace and coercive control), meaning physical violence is not required.

citations.cite: the four-category statutory definition of abuse
citations.quote: (a) For purposes of this act, "abuse" means any of the following: (1) To intentionally or recklessly cause or attempt to cause bodily injury. (2) Sexual assault. (3) To place a person in reasonable apprehension of imminent serious bodily injury to that person or to another. (4) To engage in any behavior that has been or could be enjoined pursuant to Section 6320. (b) Abuse is not limited to the actual infliction of physical injury or assault.

clauses.title: "Disturbing the Peace" and Coercive Control
clauses.body: Family Code section 6320(a) authorizes a court to enjoin a party from molesting, attacking, striking, stalking, threatening, sexually assaulting, battering, harassing, contacting, coming within a specified distance of, or disturbing the peace of the other party, among other listed acts. Section 6320(c) defines "disturbing the peace of the other party," as used in subdivision (a), as conduct that, based on the totality of the circumstances, destroys the mental or emotional calm of the other party -- committed directly or indirectly, including through a third party or electronic means. This conduct expressly includes, but is not limited to, coercive control, defined as a pattern of behavior that in purpose or effect unreasonably interferes with a person's free will and personal liberty, with examples including isolating a party from support systems, depriving a party of basic necessities, monitoring a party's movements or finances, and reproductive coercion.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what California's DVPA currently reaches under "disturbing the peace" and coercive control -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific petitioner or respondent, and many states have no equivalent coercive-control provision at all. Family Code section 6320, subdivisions (a) and (c), are provisions of a single California statutory section; this is a single statutory section (§ 6320(a), (c)); no additional independent source was found for this. The coercive-control language quoted here is the section's current text, in effect as amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 676 (SB 50), effective January 1, 2026; this research confirmed the current text directly but did not independently fetch and compare an archived pre-2025 version, so while coercive control is widely reported to have first entered this subdivision through a 2020 amendment, that specific origination is not independently confirmed here -- only that the concept, with additional examples (including reproductive coercion and immigration-status-based threats), is part of the section as currently in force.

citations.cite: the categories of conduct a court may enjoin
citations.quote: The court may issue an ex parte order enjoining a party from molesting, attacking, striking, stalking, threatening, sexually assaulting, battering, credibly impersonating as described in Section 528.5 of the Penal Code, falsely personating as described in Section 529 of the Penal Code, harassing, telephoning, including, but not limited to, making annoying telephone calls as described in Section 653m of the Penal Code, destroying personal property, contacting, either directly or indirectly, by mail or otherwise, coming within a specified distance of, or disturbing the peace of the other party, and, in the discretion of the court, on a showing of good cause, of other named family or household members.

citations.cite: the statutory definition of "disturbing the peace," including coercive control
citations.quote: As used in subdivision (a), "disturbing the peace of the other party" refers to conduct that, based on the totality of the circumstances, destroys the mental or emotional calm of the other party. This conduct may be committed directly or indirectly, including through the use of a third party, and by any method or through any means including, but not limited to, telephone, online accounts, text messages, internet-connected devices... This conduct includes, but is not limited to, coercive control, which is a pattern of behavior that in purpose or effect unreasonably interferes with a person's free will and personal liberty. Examples of coercive control include, but are not limited to, unreasonably engaging in any of the following: (1) Isolating the other party from friends, relatives, or other sources of support. (2) Depriving the other party of basic necessities. (3) Controlling, regulating, or monitoring the other party's movements, communications, daily behavior, finances, economic resources, or access to services. (4) Compelling the other party by force, threat of force, or intimidation... (5) Engaging in reproductive coercion...

clauses.title: The Standard a Court Applies
clauses.body: Family Code section 6300(a) allows a court to issue a DVPA restraining order where an affidavit or testimony, and any additional information provided under Family Code section 6306, shows to the court's satisfaction reasonable proof of a past act or acts of abuse -- and the court may issue the order based solely on the petitioner's own affidavit or testimony. Family Code section 6301(d), a separate subdivision within the same statutory part, adds that the length of time since the most recent act of abuse is not, by itself, determinative, and directs the court to consider the totality of the circumstances in deciding whether to grant or deny the petition.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Fam. Code §§ 6300 and 6301), used as real evidence of the standard California's DVPA currently applies -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific petition, or that this is the applicable standard nationwide. Correction to an initial research assumption: the "totality of the circumstances" language is often associated with section 6300 in older secondary sources and in casual research shorthand, but the current, directly-fetched text of section 6300 (as amended by Stats. 2024, Ch. 648 (AB 2024), effective January 1, 2025) does not contain that phrase -- it appears instead in the current text of the separate section 6301(d) (as amended by Stats. 2024, Ch. 652 (SB 554), effective January 1, 2025), which also states that the passage of time since the last abusive act is not by itself determinative. Because sections 6300 and 6301 are two different, independently amended statutory sections rather than subsections of one section, no single-section disclosure applies to this pairing; this clause cites both directly rather than assuming the older single-section attribution.

citations.cite: reasonable proof of a past act or acts of abuse
citations.quote: An order may be issued under this part to restrain any person for the purpose specified in Section 6220, if an affidavit or testimony and any additional information provided to the court pursuant to Section 6306, shows, to the satisfaction of the court, reasonable proof of a past act or acts of abuse. The court may issue an order under this part based solely on the affidavit or testimony of the person requesting the restraining order.

citations.cite: the totality-of-the-circumstances standard
citations.quote: The length of time since the most recent act of abuse is not, by itself, determinative. The court shall consider the totality of the circumstances in determining whether to grant or deny a petition for relief.

clauses.title: Temporary (Ex Parte) Orders and How Long a Permanent Order Lasts
clauses.body: Family Code section 6326 states that an ex parte DVPA order must be issued or denied the same day the application is submitted to the court, or the next day of judicial business if filed too late in the day for effective review, and that a petition for an ex parte order cannot be denied solely because the other party lacked notice. For a permanent order issued after notice and a hearing, Family Code section 6345(a) allows the personal conduct, stay-away, and residence exclusion provisions to last up to five years, and permits the order to be renewed -- without any showing of further abuse since the original order -- for five or more additional years, or permanently, at the court's discretion. Section 6345(c) provides that if the order's expiration date is not stated on the form, the order defaults to a three-year duration from issuance.
clauses.gap: Family Code section 6326 is a separate statutory section from Family Code section 6345, so no single-section disclosure applies to that pairing; but section 6345's subdivisions (a) and (c), cited together above, are both provisions of one statutory section (§ 6345), so this is a single statutory section for that portion; no additional independent source was found for the duration figures. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own ex parte mechanism and permanent-order duration rules -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific petition, and not a claim that an equivalent ex parte or duration scheme exists in any other state. This clause does not restate the full hearing-scheduling mechanism for an ex parte DVPA order (Family Code section 6327 cross-references the general temporary restraining order provisions commencing at Code of Civil Procedure section 240, rather than stating its own fixed number of days the way Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6(f)-(g) does for civil harassment orders), so this document does not state a specific day count for how long a DVPA temporary order remains in effect before the hearing -- that figure was not independently confirmed with a clean, self-contained citation and is not guessed at here. Notably, a DVPA order's renewal is not capped the way a civil harassment order's renewal is: section 6345(a) allows renewal "for five or more years, or permanently," which is broader than the civil harassment statute's cap of one renewal for up to five additional years.

citations.cite: the same-day ex parte order mechanism
citations.quote: An ex parte order under this article shall be issued or denied on the same day that the application is submitted to the court, unless the application is filed too late in the day to permit effective review, in which case the order shall be issued or denied on the next day of judicial business in sufficient time for the order to be filed that day with the clerk of the court. A petition for an ex parte order pursuant to this article shall not be denied solely because the other party was not provided with notice.

citations.cite: duration and renewal of a permanent order
citations.quote: In the discretion of the court, the personal conduct, stay-away, and residence exclusion orders contained in a court order issued after notice and a hearing under this article may have a duration of not more than five years... These orders may be renewed, upon the request of a party, either for five or more years, or permanently, at the discretion of the court, without a showing of further abuse since the issuance of the original order.

citations.cite: the default three-year duration when no expiration date is stated
citations.quote: The failure to state the expiration date on the face of the form creates an order with a duration of three years from the date of issuance.

clauses.title: Firearm Relinquishment Consequence
clauses.body: Family Code section 6389(a) states that a person subject to a DVPA protective order, as defined in Family Code section 6218, shall not own, possess, purchase, or receive a firearm or ammunition while the order is in effect, and that doing so is punishable under Penal Code section 29825. Section 6389(c)(1)-(2) requires the court, upon issuing a protective order, to order the respondent to relinquish any firearm or ammunition in the respondent's immediate possession or control; relinquishment must occur immediately to a requesting law enforcement officer upon service, or, if no such request is made, within 24 hours by surrender to local law enforcement or sale, transfer, or storage with a licensed gun dealer, with a receipt filed with both the court and the serving law enforcement agency within 48 hours.
clauses.gap: Family Code section 6389, subdivisions (a) and (c)(1)-(2), are provisions of a single California statutory section; no additional independent source was found for this. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific, checkable consequence that attaches to a California DVPA protective order -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific respondent, and not a claim that firearm relinquishment is a feature of every state's domestic violence restraining order. This consequence is distinct from a civil harassment order under Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6, which does not carry an equivalent statutory firearm-relinquishment requirement. Section 6389 was substantially amended effective January 1, 2026 (as added by Stats. 2024, Ch. 544, then amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 241 (SB 857)); this clause quotes the section as currently in force. This clause does not restate the section's narrow work-related and peace-officer exemption procedures under subdivisions (h) and (i), which involve separate court findings and psychological evaluation requirements not summarized here.

citations.cite: the prohibition on firearm ownership or possession while an order is in effect
citations.quote: A person subject to a protective order, as defined in Section 6218, shall not own, possess, purchase, or receive a firearm or ammunition while that protective order is in effect. A person who owns, possesses, purchases, or receives, or attempts to purchase or receive, a firearm or ammunition while the protective order is in effect is punishable pursuant to Section 29825 of the Penal Code.

citations.cite: the mandatory relinquishment procedure
citations.quote: (1) Upon issuance of a protective order, as defined in Section 6218, the court shall order the respondent to relinquish any firearm or ammunition in the respondent's immediate possession or control or subject to the respondent's immediate possession or control. (2) The relinquishment ordered pursuant to paragraph (1) shall occur by immediately surrendering the firearm or ammunition in a safe manner, upon request of a law enforcement officer, to the control of the officer, after being served with the protective order... Alternatively, if a request is not made by a law enforcement officer, the relinquishment shall occur within 24 hours of being served with the order, by either surrendering the firearm or ammunition in a safe manner to the control of local law enforcement officials, or by selling, transferring, or relinquishing for storage... to a licensed gun dealer...

clauses.title: What Governs Sublessor's Right to Sublet
clauses.body: California has a statutory chapter specifically addressing a landlord's ability to restrict a tenant from transferring the tenant's lease interest (by assignment or sublease), including a default rule that if the lease requires the landlord's consent but states no standard for it, that consent may not be unreasonably withheld. That chapter, by its own terms, applies only to a lease of real property for other than residential purposes. For a residential tenancy, whether {{sublessorName}} may sublet {{propertyAddress}} to {{subtenantName}}, and whether {{landlordName}}'s consent is required first, is controlled by the terms of the existing lease between {{landlordName}} and {{sublessorName}} (the "Master Lease") — not by that separate statutory chapter.
clauses.gap: This is a real, easy-to-miss gap rather than an assumption forced to fit: Civil Code Chapter 6 (Assignment and Sublease, §§ 1995.010-1995.340) — including its default rule that an unstandardized landlord-consent requirement may not be unreasonably withheld — is defined, by its own text, to cover only a lease of real property for other than residential purposes. There is no parallel Civil Code chapter creating a general residential right to sublet or a residential landlord-consent standard. That means a residential tenant's subletting rights genuinely are, in the main, a matter of what the Master Lease itself says: a typical residential lease either bars subletting outright, allows it only with the landlord's prior written consent, or is silent (in which case older common-law principles about a tenant's default freedom to transfer a leasehold interest can come into play). This document does not assume the Master Lease permits or forbids subletting, or that it requires consent — that has to be checked directly against the Master Lease's own text. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual scope of California's assignment/subletting statute — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific master lease. The first two citations are sections of the same statutory chapter (§§ 1995.010, 1995.020) defining that chapter's own scope; the third citation, § 1995.270's legislative findings, is an independent statutory source that separately corroborates the chapter's commercial-only focus and its historical basis in the Kendall v. Ernest Pestana litigation. The fourth citation goes further still: it's Kendall's own text (verified directly against CourtListener's opinion record, not a paraphrase), and in a footnote the California Supreme Court itself expressly declined to say whether the commercial-lease consent principles it was announcing in that case apply to residential leases at all — meaning even the single most important California case on landlord-consent standards pointedly leaves the residential question open, rather than answering it.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1995.010 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the assignment/sublease restrictions chapter is nonresidential-only
citations.quote: This chapter applies to transfer of a tenant’s interest in a lease of real property for other than residential purposes.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1995.020(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, "lease" is defined as nonresidential for this chapter
citations.quote: “Lease” means a lease or sublease of real property for other than residential purposes, and includes modifications and other agreements affecting a lease.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1995.270(a)(1)-(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, legislative findings confirming the chapter concerns commercial real property leases
citations.quote: (a) The Legislature finds and declares: (1) It is the public policy of the state and fundamental to the commerce and economic development of the state to enable and facilitate freedom of contract by the parties to commercial real property leases. (2) The parties to commercial real property leases must be able to negotiate and conduct their affairs in reasonable reliance on the rights and protections given them under the laws of the state. (3) Until the case of Kendall v. Ernest Pestana, Inc., 40 Cal. 3d 488 (1985), and its predecessor, Cohen v. Ratinoff, 147 Cal. App. 3d 321 (1983), the parties to commercial real property leases could reasonably rely on the law of the state to provide that if a lease restriction requires the landlord’s consent for transfer of the tenant’s interest in the lease but provides no standard for giving or withholding consent, the landlord’s consent may be unreasonably withheld.

citations.case: Kendall v. Ernest Pestana, Inc., 40 Cal.3d 488, 493 n.1 (1985) (opinion text via CourtListener)
citations.cite: California Supreme Court, expressly declining to decide whether its commercial-lease rule extends to residential leases
citations.quote: We are presented only with a commercial lease and therefore do not address the question whether residential leases are controlled by the principles articulated in this opinion.

clauses.title: Assignment vs. Sublease
clauses.body: Subletting {{propertyAddress}} to {{subtenantName}} is legally different from assigning the Master Lease to {{subtenantName}}, even though both are ways {{sublessorName}} can transfer some interest in the leased property to someone else. In a sublease, {{sublessorName}} transfers only part of its remaining interest under the Master Lease — for example, a shorter term than what remains, or only part of the space — and remains a tenant to {{landlordName}} while also taking on a landlord-like role toward {{subtenantName}}. In a full assignment, {{sublessorName}} would instead transfer its entire remaining interest under the Master Lease to the new party, who would then generally deal with {{landlordName}} directly going forward in {{sublessorName}}'s place. This document is a sublease, not an assignment: {{sublessorName}} keeps its position as tenant under the Master Lease and remains directly responsible to {{landlordName}} for compliance with it, as described elsewhere in this document.
clauses.gap: This distinction is confirmed directly against primary case text, not a secondary-source paraphrase. Kendall v. Ernest Pestana, Inc. (1985) 40 Cal.3d 488, 493 n.2, states it in so many words: "The difference between an assignment and a sublease is that an assignment transfers the lessee's entire interest in the property whereas a sublease transfers only a portion of that interest, with the original lessee retaining a right of reentry at some point during the unexpired term of the lease." Kendall cites, for that same point, Hartman Ranch Co. v. Associated Oil Co. (1937) 10 Cal.2d 232, 242-243 — an independent, older California Supreme Court decision (about an oil-and-gas lease, not real estate generally) that states the distinction on its own terms and explains the doctrine behind it: California follows the "Massachusetts rule" that a transferor who reserves a right of reentry for breach of conditions keeps a "contingent reversionary interest," which is what keeps the transfer from operating as a full assignment of the unexpired term — a sublease results instead. Both quotes below were read directly from each case's opinion text (via CourtListener), not assumed from a secondary summary. Neither case involved a residential tenancy — Kendall was a commercial hangar-space dispute and Hartman Ranch an oil-and-gas lease dispute — but the assignment/sublease distinction itself is treated in both opinions as general property-law doctrine rather than something specific to a commercial lease, and Civil Code § 1995.020(e) (part of the nonresidential-only Chapter 6 discussed under "What Governs Sublessor's Right to Sublet" above) independently confirms that California statutory law also recognizes assignment and sublease as distinct categories of lease transfer, even though it doesn't itself spell out the substantive test. That third citation quotes two subsections of the same statutory section, § 1995.020(a) and (e) — disclosed here because it is one section read twice, not two independent statutory sources, so the real independent authority for the doctrinal test itself is the case law above, with the statute offered only as corroboration that California law recognizes the two categories at all. This is one state's case law, used as real evidence of the actual doctrinal test — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific document.

citations.case: Kendall v. Ernest Pestana, Inc., 40 Cal.3d 488, 493 n.2 (1985) (opinion text via CourtListener)
citations.cite: California Supreme Court, the assignment/sublease distinction stated directly
citations.quote: Since the present case involves an assignment rather than a sublease, we will speak primarily in terms of assignments. However, our holding applies equally to subleases. The difference between an assignment and a sublease is that an assignment transfers the lessee's entire interest in the property whereas a sublease transfers only a portion of that interest, with the original lessee retaining a right of reentry at some point during the unexpired term of the lease.

citations.case: Hartman Ranch Co. v. Associated Oil Co., 10 Cal.2d 232, 242-243 (1937) (opinion text via CourtListener)
citations.cite: California Supreme Court, independently stating the same distinction and its doctrinal basis
citations.quote: The generally stated distinction between an assignment and a sublease is that an assignment transfers the entire unexpired term. ... [W]e are committed to the so-called Massachusetts rule that where the transferor reserves the right of reentry for breach of conditions he has a "contingent reversionary interest" which prevents his transfer from operating as an assignment of the whole of the unexpired term. Instead, a sublease arises.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1995.020(a), (e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, "transfer" is defined to include both assignment and sublease as distinct categories, and a sublease creates a "sublandlord"
citations.quote: (a) “Landlord” includes a tenant who is a sublandlord under a sublease. ... (e) “Transfer” of a tenant’s interest in a lease means an assignment, sublease, or other voluntary or involuntary transfer or encumbrance of all or part of a tenant’s interest in the lease.

clauses.title: Sublessor Remains Bound to Landlord
clauses.body: Entering into this sublease with {{subtenantName}} does not release {{sublessorName}} from any of its obligations to {{landlordName}} under the Master Lease. {{sublessorName}} remains fully responsible to {{landlordName}} for rent, upkeep, and all other Master Lease obligations for {{propertyAddress}}, regardless of whether {{subtenantName}} pays rent on time, complies with the Master Lease's terms, or vacates early. If {{subtenantName}} breaches this sublease or damages the property, {{sublessorName}} — not {{landlordName}} — bears that loss in the first instance, unless {{sublessorName}} separately recovers it from {{subtenantName}}. At the same time, under this sublease {{sublessorName}} effectively stands in {{landlordName}}'s shoes toward {{subtenantName}}, taking on landlord-like responsibilities to {{subtenantName}} while remaining, itself, a tenant to {{landlordName}}.
clauses.gap: This is a well-established rule of California landlord-tenant law, confirmed directly against primary case text. The California Supreme Court has stated it plainly: "the original lessee remains liable to the lessor as a surety even if the lessor consents to the assignment and the assignee expressly assumes the obligations of the lease" (Kendall v. Ernest Pestana, Inc. (1985) 40 Cal.3d 488, 500) — a sentence that itself cites, for that exact point, two of the Supreme Court's own earlier decisions, so the underlying rule rests on at least three independent sources, not one restated citation. One of those two, Peiser v. Mettler (1958) 50 Cal.2d 594, 602, was independently pulled and confirms the rule in even more direct language (quoting an earlier case, De Hart v. Allen): an assignment or sublease "does not release the lessee from his obligations even though the lessor consents to the assignment," and "the express assumption by the assignee of obligations under the lease" doesn't change that, because "as between the lessor and the lessee[,] the latter remains a primary obligor under his express contract to pay rent." All of this case law states the rule in the assignment context specifically, but nothing in the reasoning turns on the assignment/sublease distinction described elsewhere in this document — a sublessor, who transfers only part of the leasehold interest and keeps an ongoing tenancy relationship with the landlord, has at least as much of a continuing contractual relationship with the landlord as an assignor does, so the same primary-obligor/surety-liability logic applies with equal or greater force to a sublease. Separately, Civil Code § 1995.020(a), (d) — part of the nonresidential-only Chapter 6 discussed under "What Governs Sublessor's Right to Sublet" above — independently corroborates the underlying structure by defining a sublessor as simultaneously a "tenant" to the original landlord and a "sublandlord" to the subtenant, consistent with the sublessor's obligations to the landlord surviving the sublease. That statutory citation likewise quotes two subsections of the same section, § 1995.020(a) and (d) — disclosed here because it is one section read twice, not two independent statutory sources; the independent authority for the liability rule itself is the case law above, with the statute offered only as structural corroboration. This is one state's case law, used as real evidence of the actual liability rule — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific master lease — and it says nothing about whatever separate indemnity or reimbursement rights Sublessor may or may not have against Subtenant; the actual Master Lease's own default and remedies provisions, not this general default description, control the mechanics of any actual dispute.

citations.case: Kendall v. Ernest Pestana, Inc., 40 Cal.3d 488, 500 (1985) (opinion text via CourtListener)
citations.cite: California Supreme Court, original tenant remains liable as a surety after transferring the lease
citations.quote: The lessor's interests are also protected by the fact that the original lessee remains liable to the lessor as a surety even if the lessor consents to the assignment and the assignee expressly assumes the obligations of the lease. (Peiser v. Mettler (1958) 50 Cal.2d 594, 602 [328 P.2d 953, 74 A.L.R.2d 1]; Samuels v. Ottinger (1915) 169 Cal. 209, 212 [146 P. 638].)

citations.case: Peiser v. Mettler, 50 Cal.2d 594, 602 (1958) (opinion text via CourtListener)
citations.cite: California Supreme Court, independently stating the original tenant remains a primary obligor to the landlord
citations.quote: Ordinarily an assignment of a lease does not release the lessee from his obligations even though the lessor consents to the assignment. ... Nor does the express assumption by the assignee of obligations under the lease affect the liability of the lessee to the lessor. ... but as between the lessor and the lessee the latter remains a primary obligor under his express contract to pay rent.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1995.020(a), (d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, a sublessor is both a "tenant" to the landlord and a "sublandlord" (landlord) to the subtenant
citations.quote: (a) “Landlord” includes a tenant who is a sublandlord under a sublease. ... (d) “Tenant” includes a subtenant or assignee.

clauses.title: Subtenant Has No Direct Relationship with Landlord
clauses.body: As a general default rule, {{subtenantName}} does not step into a direct legal relationship with {{landlordName}} merely by virtue of this sublease. {{subtenantName}}'s rights and obligations run to {{sublessorName}}, not to {{landlordName}}, and {{landlordName}}'s remedies for a breach of the Master Lease generally run against {{sublessorName}}, not directly against {{subtenantName}}. This sublease does not, by itself, give {{subtenantName}} the right to enforce the Master Lease against {{landlordName}}, or give {{landlordName}} the right to collect rent or otherwise enforce lease terms directly against {{subtenantName}} for {{propertyAddress}}, unless the Master Lease, {{landlordName}}'s written consent to this sublease, or a separate agreement signed by all three parties provides otherwise.
clauses.gap: This no-privity default is a real, well-established rule of California property law, confirmed directly against primary case text. Hartman Ranch Co. v. Associated Oil Co. (1937) 10 Cal.2d 232, 242, states it directly: "This doctrine as to sublessees generally is well settled. ... A sublessee is liable only to his own lessor, that is, the sub-lessor, since he does not acquire the whole estate, but only a portion of the unexpired term." A few pages later the same opinion explains the doctrinal mechanism — that the sublessee's relationship with the original landlord lacks privity of estate (the property-law relationship that, for an assignee in full possession, makes the assignee directly answerable to the landlord on the lease covenants): "as to both sublessee in possession, and the assignee who has terminated his possession[,] there is no privity of estate with the lessor." Both quotes below are from the same 1937 case rather than independently authored sources; that case is, however, corroborated by a second, independent source: Civil Code § 822 extends a landlord's lease remedies — for breach of a lease agreement, or for recovery of possession — expressly to the tenant's "assignees," but its text never mentions subtenants or sublessees at all, which is consistent with (though not itself an express statement of) the same no-privity default for subtenants that Hartman Ranch states directly. Hartman Ranch was an oil-and-gas lease dispute, not a residential tenancy, but the privity principle it applies is general California property-law doctrine rather than something specific to that lease type. This is one state's case law, used as real evidence of the actual default rule — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific master lease. Nothing here should be read as guaranteeing that no direct relationship can ever arise in a particular deal — a landlord's written consent to a sublease, a separate non-disturbance or attornment agreement, or specific master lease language can each create direct rights or obligations between the landlord and the subtenant, and the actual Master Lease and any consent documents should be checked for that possibility.

citations.case: Hartman Ranch Co. v. Associated Oil Co., 10 Cal.2d 232, 242 (1937) (opinion text via CourtListener)
citations.cite: California Supreme Court, a subtenant is liable only to the sublessor, not the original landlord
citations.quote: Defendant contends that as a sublessee it is not liable to the original lessor in damages for breach of covenants in the parent lease. This doctrine as to sublessees generally is well settled. ... A sublessee is liable only to his own lessor, that is, the sub-lessor, since he does not acquire the whole estate, but only a portion of the unexpired term.

citations.case: Hartman Ranch Co. v. Associated Oil Co., 10 Cal.2d 232, 244 (1937) (opinion text via CourtListener)
citations.cite: California Supreme Court, a subtenant lacks privity of estate with the original landlord
citations.quote: An assignee in possession is liable to the parent lessor by virtue of privity of estate (covenants running with the land), and it is not ordinarily necessary to consider whether by virtue of an agreement of assumption there is also privity of contract between them. But where the assignee is no longer in possession, the privity of estate is terminated ..., and if he is liable to the lessor it is by virtue of his contract of assumption. Since as to both sublessee in possession, and the assignee who has terminated his possession there is no privity of estate with the lessor, cases involving an assignee who has assumed the parent lease, but is no longer in possession, will indicate the rule applicable also to sublessees who assume the parent lease.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 822 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, a landlord's lease remedies extend to the tenant's "assignees" — subtenants are not mentioned
citations.quote: Whatever remedies the lessor of any real property has against his immediate lessee for the breach of any agreement in the lease, or for recovery of the possession, he has against the assignees of the lessee, for any cause of action accruing while they are such assignees, except where the assignment is made by way of security for a loan, and is not accompanied by possession of the premises.
